THE HUMAN AUCTION.

-- Ho! here are lives by the score to sell, Up to the platform, gents, and bid; Make me an offer, they'll pay you well— AU of 'em ripe for the coffin lid. Here is a woman, pinched and pale, Plying her needle for daily bread: Give me a shirt for her—more on sale, Dying! gentlemen--dying !—dead! A family, six in number' here, Fresh from a cellar in Somers Town; Mother her sixth confinement near, Father and brats with fever down. 'Twas pestilence spoke then, was it not? "An open sewer," I think he said; Well, his offer shall buy the lot, • Dying! gentlemen—dying !—dead! Novi', good customers, here's a chance; A thousand men in the prime of life, Wielders of musket, sword, and lance, Armed and drilled for the deadly strife. General Warfare lifts his hand—and "A bullet for each" cries the gent in red. No offer but his—fast flows the sand, Dying! gentlemen—dying! dead. A body of toilers, worn and weak, Clerks and curates and writing men— Look at the flush of each sunken cheek, Mark the fingers that grasp the pen! Come, good gentlemen. can't we deal? Has Drudgery's eye for bargains fled? He offers, at least, the price of a meal— Dying! gentlemen—dying! dead! GEORGE R. SIMS.

A baby sister has lately come to a certain household. The children, hearing that the baby was to be called after a friend of the family whom they have always heard ad- dressed as Miss Agnes, gave the title to the baby. "What is the name of your baby sister?" asked a lady on the street car. "Her name is Miss Agnes," said Jack, gravely. "And how old is she?" the lady went on. "Oh, she isn't any old; she is all new. Don't you know about babies?" Some European ladies passing through Constantinople paid a visit to a certain high Turkish functionary. The host offered them refreshments, including a great variety of sweetmeats, always taking care to give one of the ladies double the quantity he gave to the others. Flat- tered by this marked attention, she put the question through the interpreter—" Why do you serve me more liberally than the rest?" "Because you have a larger mouth," was the straightforward reply. • Maur PUT HER FOOT IN IT.—" Mary," said a pro- minent Cincinnati gentleman to his wife a few mornings ago, just before leaving for his place of business, "Mary, [expect a couple of gentlemen will be out here trr-day to I look at our place with a view of buying. Don't be care- less with them and neglect to show them all the good points about the premises. If you are a little discreet now we can get a good price for the property." "I understand, lovey, I'll not neglect them,' hearing which • the " lovey" departed. Ia the course of the day two gentlemen called, and the Mrs. gave them all the aid possible in inspecting the place. No real estate dealer could ever have been more valuable in describing the property in an auction down town thau was this little spouse. ," Why, gentlemen," said she, "we have ac- tually received repeated offers of $60,000 for-this pro- perty, and have held it all along to be worth every cent of $75,000." That night, as the husband entered his home, he said, "I was sorry, to-day, but those gentlemen had some down-town engagement, so that they could not come out." " What'sthat you say ?" exclaimed the wife. "I said those gentlemen couldn't come out." "But they did, though, and I tell you I cracked up the place to them. I verily believe I made them think the old rookery was worth $60,800." "How did they look?" asked the husband. The wife described them, when the husband threw up both hands and yelled: "Mary, you have undone me completely. You have been talking to the assessors !" Aln erican. COMPOSING Swim ES IN. DREAMS.—Mr. R. L. Stevensog is said to have given a New York Herald reporter tWI following account of how he wrote some of his stories,l including the famous "Dr. Jekyll" story :—" On one occasion I was very hard up for money, and I felt that I I had to do something. I thought and thought, and tried I hard to find a subject to write abotit: At night I I dreamed the story, not precisely as it is written, for of course there are always stupidities in dreams, but prac- tically it came to me as a gift, and what makes it appear more odd is that I am quite in the habit of dreaming stories. Thus, not long ago, I dreamed the story of ()Irina,' which appeared in my volume, 'The Merry Men,' and I have at the present moment two unwritten stories which I likewise dreamed. The fact is that lam so much in the habit of making stories that I go on making them while asleep quite as hard, apparently, as when lam awake. They sometimes come to me in the form of nightmares, in so far that they make me cry out aloud. That lam never deceived by them. Even when fast asleep I know that it is I who am inventing, and when I cry out it is with gratification to know that the story is so good. So soon as I awake, and it always awakens me when I get on a good thing, I set to work and put it together. For instance, all I dreamed about Dr. Jekyll was that one man was being pressed into a cabinet, when he swallowed a drug, and changed into another being. I awoke, and said at once that I had found the missing link for which I had been looking so 10r,,z. and before I again went to sleep almost every detail of the story, as it stands, was clear to me. Of course, writing it was another thing." A LARGE CLOCIL—The Waterbury Watch Company, Hartford. Connecticut, has almost completed a large clock:which in its mechanism is said to surpass the well- known Strassburg clock. This clock is 18 feet high, with a base of 7 feet; its width is 8 feet, and it is 6 feet deep. Five years have been occupied in its construction; sometimes four, at others five, men have been engaged on the work. Time is indicated in the usual manner, by hours, minutes, and seconds; in addition, half- seconds, eighths, sixteenths, and one-thirty-seconds of I a second. The days of the year, month, and week may also be taken from the dial. The number of wheels, I • pinions, springs, and other parts of the mechanism is ' legion, all of which contribute to most wonderful and amusing exhibitions of historical events. The several phases of the moon are indicated. The entire sys- tem of the planets and solar systems are shown in , perfect form and in all the varied revolutions. Many hundred figures represent distinguished men of all nations. These figures are carved in wood from correct likenesses, and are said to be most complete representa- tions. The signers of the Declaration of Independence assembled as represented in history, the Cabinet of Lin- coln when the emancipation proclamation was signed, the surrender of Lee at Appomattox, several scenes at the Centennial at Philadelphia in 1878, and noted scenes and historical events as represented in the Bible have a pro- minent place. Shaksperian plays are set out with characters true to the representations of the author and the modern setting at the theatres, with dress and cos- tume to correspond. Figures and fashions of dress, both ancient and modern, down to the latest period, are among the curiosities. A multitude of amusing scenes will fill out the measure of this wonderful clock, which is to be exhibited in several of the leading cities of the United States. Its ultimate resting-place is not yet known.—lron. LETTERS OF THE GREAT NAPOLEON.—Some of the un- published letters of the Great Napoleon collected by Baron A. Du Casse have Just made their appearance in Paris in a small volume entitled "Supplement. a la Cor- respondence de Napoleon Premier." Few of them, of • course (the _Daily Telegraph's correspondent remarks), are by the Emperor's own hand. He was in the habit of dictating to his secretaries, and adding and altering in an almost illegible manner. Even when Napoleon did . attempt a letter off his own pen he rarely finished it himself, and to the last his spelling was anything but faultless. In one of these epistles, indited at the Mill-

. , tary School at Brienne when he was only fifteen, he gave his uncle his opinion of his brother Joseph. "He is desirous of serving the King, but he is very wrong, for several reasons. In the first place, as my dear father re- marks, he is not bold enough to confront the perils of an ' action. His weak health does not allow him to support the fatigues of a campaign, and my brother only looks at the garrison side of a soldier's life. Yes, my dear brother will be a very good garrison officer, well made, with a light heart, consequently apt at frivolous com- pliments, and with his talents he will always get on well in society; but in a fieht---2 That is what my dear father doubts." From the first Napoleon had his eye on his brothers. Here is a short epistle addressed to Jerome in August, 1802 :—" I have received your letter, ' Monsieur l'Enseigne de marine. I hope I shall soon hear that you are ou board your corvette on the open sea, which should be your path to glory. Die young—l quite. agree with that; but not if you have lived without glory, without being of use to your country, without . leaving any trace of your existence; for this is as if you had never existed." In a pr:vious letter he had told Jerome to toil hard, to, get up the masts and study the different parts of the ship, and, above all, to let no one else do his work. He had impressed on min that he must .seize every opportunity of distinguishing himself and to stick to the navy. The last letter to which I shall draw your attention was written to Joseph in January, 1809. "I am not pleased with the Madrid police. Befliard is very weak. With the Spaniards you must be severe. I have had fifteen of the wor4 arrested and shot here. Have thirty arrested at Madrid. When I loft an investi- gation was going on, and they were on the point of being seized. When treated with mildness, this canaille deems itself invulnerable. When a few are shot, it begins to grow disgusted with the game, and becomes submissive and humble, as it should be." These side-lights (the cor- respondent observes) contribute to a true estimate of the man.

RUNCORN RIFLE VOLUNTEERS ; DIS- TRIBUTION OF PRIZES. The annual concert and distribution of prizes in connection with the F and 0 (Runcorn) Companies of the Earl of. Chester's Rifles took place on Tues- day night in the Drill Hall, Greenway-road. An audience of large proportions assembled, and the proceedings were of a most enjoyable character. Mr. J. Brundrit. J.P., occupied the chair, and on the platform were Major Razlehurst, Captain Jolliffe, Captain Timmins, Lieut. Rhodes, and the TLev. W. Preston, M.A. The Chairman, after expressing his pleasure at presi- ding, said it must lkegratifying to the officers and men to see such a large attendance showing sympathy with them. It would act as a '4imulu3 to increase tlieir effi- ciency. From statistics before them, however, there was nothingt4 complain of in regard to efficiency. The present strength of the ' companies was ).74., and there were 173 efficient, which he thought was very favour- able. (Applause.) Alluding to the commencement of the volunteer movement 28 years ago, with the object of repelling an invasion from France, Mr. Brundrit said in the first year, 1859, fifty thousand who had been mere civilians were enrolled hi the United Kingdom. Runcorn was not the last on that occasion to show her loyalty. (Applause.) On the 9th December, 1859, he was one of the first 63 men who were enrolled members of the first corps in Runcorn. (Applause.) Though he did not wish to be egotistical, hq did not think there-was a finer lot of men got together' on any Occasion, and he thought they would agree with him when he told them that the average height of the :sixty- three men in this then small town I 51t. 9tin. This showed that there were very few lilipu- titians amongst them. (Applause.) However, height did not always do what was needed; it 11'as the heart that was the great thing ; -and he doubted not that the volunteers at the present time would not be found want- ing if their services were required. Mr. Brunner alluded to the physical and moral advantage of a connection with the volunteers, who had to perform exercises and drill, and had also to undergo a certain amount of self- restraint and self-denial. 'He did not think there were any of the 'original 63 alit in the corps. He thought there was one who joined in the following year, 1860, so that he was a veteran, but as he was a very well-known man he would not mention his name. In conclusion, Mr. Brundrit referred to the loss the corps had sustained by the death of one of its, young officers, a young man fuu of promise, vitality, aid life, and one wom it might reasonably be expected would have been -connected with the corps for many years to come. It was ordained otherwise, and that his loss was felt very much was shown by the large attendance of volunteers and general public at his funeral, and he was sure he,would not ap- peal in vain foetheir sympathy on behalf of the now childless widow.' After a few musical selections, Mrs. Hazlehurst, wife of Major Hazlehurst, distributed the prizes to the suc- cessful volunteers. Captain Jolliffe proposed a hearty vote of thanks. to Mrs. Hazlehurst for her kindness, and was accorded with enthusiasm. Major Hazlehurst replied on behalf of his wife in a few well-chosen remarks. He felt now that there was a new era in his careeras a volunteer. Having attained his majority he had to give up the command of the Runcorn Volunteers, and it was with very great regret that he did so. However, it was a great pleasure to him that he had to hand over the command to such an officer as Capt. Joiliffe. There was a duty owing to all the non- commissioned officers of the F and 0 Companies of the Runcorn Volunteers. In the latter part of 1880 they asked him (Major Hazlehurst) if he would become an officer in the corps. At that time, as many of them would remember, there were no officers at all. After some consideration he accepted, on one condition, and that was that they promised him faithfully that they would do everything possible to bring up the corps to the standard they told him it had attained in years gone by. He believed they had worked fer that end. The average strength of the companies during the past six years had been 180; the average strength for the six years previously had been 115; so that there was a marked increasie of 65. There was one fact he felt deeply lat the present time, and that was that he had unfor- tunately to hand over the companies at less strength than they had been during the past six years. He called upon the non-commissioned officers to aid Captain Jolliffe in doing what they promised they would do for him, to bring up the strength of the companies to its maximum. Let them have 200 efficient men in Run- corn. There was no reason why it should not be so. They had in Runcorn young men always willing to join the band; he only wished they would join the corps. He wished the non-commissioned officers to work for Captain Jolliffe as they had worked for him during the time he had the detachment. (Applause.) Captain Timmins then moved that a cordial vote of thanks be given to the numerous donors of 4 p,rizes and subscribers, and also to the ladies and gentlemen who had contributed to that evening's entertainment. The Rev. W. Preston, M.A., seconded the proposition, which was heartily carried. A vote of thanks was afterwards accorded to the chair- man on the motion of Captain Jolliffe. During the evening a glee party consisting of Miss Jones, Miss Birkett, Mr. R. Morris, and Mr. J. Birkett, rendered several glees in capital style. Mr. R. Morris, Mr. C. Pownall, and Mr. George Clegg contributed songs, the vocalisation of the gentlemen being Mitch appre- ciated. Mr. Clegg was rewarded with an encore, and he greatly anthsed the audience by an original and humour- ous account of the volunteer movement in Runcorn. The volunteer band also rendered Several selections of music. The prize list is as follows COMPANY DRILL COMPETITION. Open to all efficient members of the detachment. WARRINGTON LITERARY AND PHILOOPHICAL SOCIETY. The first meeting of another session of this society was held on Tuesday evening in, the Lecture Room, at the Museum, when a paper was read by the president (Mr. R. Davies) on "A visit to the Riviera." Mr. Davies presided, and there was a fair attendance of members.—The PRESIDENT said that was the first meeting of the 18th session of that society, and he regretted to say that the past session had been sad- dened by two events. First, they lost by death Mr. Charles Broadbent, and recently they had lost the Rev. R. Pitcher, B.A. Both of these had been attendants at those lectures, both of them had been contributors of papers, and both, rather singular to say, members of their Council. He felt sure he should be merely anticipating their wishes in requesting their secretary, who was a personal friend of Mr. Filcher, to convey to his surviving relatives the feelings of regret with which last week they received the melancholy intelligence of his death. (Hear, hear.) He (the chairman) hoped the coming ses- sion might not be marked by any such event.—Mr. J. R. Yomso (lion. sec.) said he should like to remind those visitors who were in the habit of favouring them with. their company at those meetings that it was so easy to attain membership of their society that there was little or no excuse for anyone remaining outside. There was nothing more necessary than giving the name to one of the secretaries' after which the name would ,be pro- posed at the next meeting, and, so far as he remembered, they had never yet had to resort to the use of the ballot, nor had anybody, in his recollection, been blackballed. He might saythat the influx of young members who would assist, not only by Iheir presence, but by giving papers would be a very material help to them. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the work of the coming session, he; said that up to Christmas they were quite decided. At the next meeting the Rev. Gibson Smith would give them a paper on Plato, and he need hardly say they' would have an intellectual treat. (Hear, hear.) A paper-would also be given by Dr. Hurter, chemist, of Widnes, on the subject, he believed, of "Nitrogen," and those who had heard Dr. Hurter lecture would know how admirable his illustrations were, and in that case he might say they would have a scientifid treat. A paper would also be given by Mr. Greg on one of the American poets, and they would also be glad to know that the pre- sident's brother would give them a paper—which had long been angled for—on "Dante." (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Young) did not think that during his connection with the society they had ever had a paper on such a subject as that. Mr. Young then proposed that the fol- lowing persons be members of the society :—C. E. Rich- mond, surgeon; John Burgess, solicitor; S. Taylor, soli- citor; R. Fairclough, James Cannel, surgeon; John. Nun- nerley, T. Fletcher, J. J. Sanderson, W. C. Copeland, Rey. F. Slater, Rev. J. J. Langham, and W. Dimmelow. —Mr. DAVIES then read his paper which was a long but interesting description of the places visited and the ob- jects seen during a holiday on the Riviera. With regard to the natives of that part of France, the peasants, he said, are most hardworking, both male and female, and receive for wages, the men from two to three francs, and the women about half those sutns—a low return for their labour, when it is considered that nothing is cheaper than it is in England, not even bread • sugar is about sevenpence a pound, and coffee about half-a-crown. They are civil to strangers, but always agree with you in any opinion you express, thinking to please you. The land system is very different to our own; where the farmers are not the owners of the land they till and irri- gate, for irrigation is a most important feature. The landlords and they work together on the metayer system, I whereby the landlord finds land, implements, and sepds, in return for the tenant's labour, and is paid so many days' service, and by a share of every product. The soil is mostly a strong reddish brown or terracotta col- oured loan, being the earth and disintegrated rock, washed down by the torrents of ages, wanting water only to produce great fertility, and it is not too much to say that there is not a level field—in fact, nothing in the shape of a field, along the whole country. All is spade work, ploughing not being practicable. Terraces and walls, walls and terraces, climb to the tops of the nearer mountain spurs, exciting absolute wonder at the toilafid, expense required to build them. One French economist declares that nothing grown there could ever pay for the labour and expense of such exertions. They are nothing less than monuments of the struggles of life against fam- ine, and of poverty against the forces of nature. There is not an inclf of waste land to be seen where cultivation is practicable, and the narrowest possible width is al- lowed to the footpaths, which afford the only roads ex- cept the main highroads. No cow is ever seen, though occasionally a man leading, not driving, a few tall long- eared sheep, in Scriptural fashion, is met with. Fences are all but unknown, and a general air of untidiness and bareness (to English eyes) characterizes the orchardless and gardenless farms. The French law, of course, pre- vails, by which land is divided and sub-divided at every death, so that you are at no loss to account for the small plots you come across in your rambles amongst the hills. At the conclusion of the paper a hearty vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Davies, on the motion of Mr. T. G. Rylands, seconded by Mr. J. Dun.

CO-OPERATIVE Cowonass.—The Marquis of Ripon pre- sided on Saturday at a conference and at a public meet- held at Flebden bridge in connection with the - north- western section of the Co-operative Union. Adverting to the great subject of discussion for the next coMgress, Lord Ripon strongly advocated the sharing of profits amongst the workers, whose claim was, he said, primary to that of the consumer. Co-operative institutions were established to afford the working classes means to make the most of their labour, and at the same time to give them a very valuable industrial training. If those moral ends were lost sight of in the movement it must inevitably fail to attain the objects with which it started and would deserve to fall under the censures which had been directed against it by the Socialist party in London. _ .

Aw went to reych unideltwn off th' shelf, an' as soon as aw'd getten houd o' th' dish, th' stoo' top, pled o'er ut aw wur stonding on, an' deawn aw went, smashin' th' dish i' mony a scoor o' pieces.

"Arto makkin' broth, Sammy?" he axt when he seed th' pen uppoth foyar. Hoo wernt satisfied till boo went an axt urn who they'd bowt um off, an boo slept Tarry little that neet for thinkin abeawt urn." who had this question at heart ought to push forward with all their will to get Home Rule out of the way. Last of all was a slibject which had to do with religious equality. Scotland and Wales were more particularly concerned. As to disestablishment in Scotland and Wales, the principle had long age been determined by the Liberal party. The Welsh question must be ripe, when 28 out of 30 members were agreed on the subject. Sootland must endeavour to secure the same unanimity. Finally, Mr. Gladstone said itwa.s thought that he should ; proceed further—to bind himself in determining the pre- cise manner in which all the principal en- actments of a future bill for the government ; of Ireland should' be framed. He was not I prepared, and did not intend to bind himself. I He had said with regard to many imporW,nt subjects ; that had created great diderence of opium* that 'he for , his part would not allow any proposals he had been a I party to making, Or any •opmions he might personally lean to, to beoome impediments in the way of the settle- ; ment of that peat question, provided that settlement I .complied with the conditions originally laid down, and provi. it had the acoeptance of Ireland, for without that Yb dance no one would be fool enough to so on with the certain knowledge that he would lose the fruits I of his labours, provided that it did nothing to impair but everything to strengthen and consolidate the unity of the Empire, and provided also that no just claim of a minority was neglected. He had given a wide and sten: gent pledge in saying that neither as to the representa- tion of Ireland, nor as to the use of the Imperial credit In the purchasenf Irish land, nor ,as to the delegation, instead of the surrender, of powers; as to the mode, the particulars,and times under-which the administra- tive system of Ireland was to be altered from one that was &iglish and anti-national in spirit to one that was Irislaand national in spirit—to the whole Of these pro- positions the declarations he had made still applied in the fullest sense. Under his elan the British Parliament was the ultimate power. For the arrest of 'injustice in Ireland the British Parliament had the very fullest power of interfering; and though he hoped the inter- ference -would be infrequent, yet undoubtedly the power was there. As to Ulster, on which Lord Hartington had imiitedlim to declare himself, he declined to walk into strap. How; could he do so until he knew the opinions (if ;his 'friends and colleagues, of the Irish niembers of Leinster, Munster, and Connaught, and even of Ulster itself ? Mr. Gladstone read telegrams stating that Dr. Kane, the leader of the Ulster Orange party, had reptt- tliated the idea of the separation of Ulster; while Colonel 'Saunderson had repudiated Mr. Chamberlain's land scheme. Since- the promulgation of the Home Rule policy, the conduct of the Irish people in self-restraint and moderation had on the whole been most laudable. At present they were under circumstances of peculiar provo- cationiand what he was anxious for was thatthat prove- nation should not lead them into violence or unlawful acts. The best advice he could give to the Irish- man was to shun outrage as he would slitin poison. ((Cheers,) MR. GLADSTONE AT DERBY..

Mr. Gladstone received a deputation of the Irish in- habitants Of Nottingham on Thursday before leaving for 'Derby,:and in reply to an address he expressed the be- lief that the Protestant people of Ireland would yet take . advantage of 'Home Rule. He was loudly 'cheered on leaving Nottingham, and he met with a hearty reception .at'Derby,where many thousands of people hadassembled in the streets. Addressing a meeting in the Drill Hall at Herby, the right hon. gentleman said he believed the field of Iriah controversy was narrowing in the 'vital sense that the forces to which the Liberal partrwere opposed were narrowing, whilst their own forces were 'multiplying and extending. It was com- •monly said he was co-operating with men Whom he had • denounced as marching through rapine and murder to the disruption of the Empire. He had used that descrip- tion; but &was not a question now whether he was 'right or wrong. The circumstances had changed. He did not believe there was now a single Irish member who contemplated or desired dismemberment. He wanted; a union of hearts, and not of paper and parchment. The Coercion Bill of last ses- sion was aimed, not at the suppression of crime, but at the liberty of the press and the public, • and for that reason the Liberals opposed it. He repudia- ted the charges of inconsistency which had been levelled at him on this point. He thought the time had arrived Ifor the•adoption of a better way than coercion. He did not want 'to drive in the disease which Ireland suffered from, and he believed the people of Great Britain were anxious to settle what had been so long a formidable difficulty. It was, he said, an utter mistake to suppose that the plan of the Liberals would he 'in any degree dangerous either to Ireland or to this country. Sir IWilliam Harcourt, M.P., also addressed the meeting,
UNTVERSITY LOCAL LECTURES. PROFESSOR BOYD DAWKINS AT WARRINGTON.

On Monday evening, the first of a course of eight 'lectures in connection with the University Exten- sion Movement was delivered in the Co-operative Hall, Warrington, by Professor Boyd Dawkins. The , -subject of the lecture was "The Ancient geography and Geological History of Britain." Mr. T. G. Itylands presided, and there was a large attendance. —The CHA/RMAN, in introducing Professor Daw- kins, said he wished to commend to the a:tention of the audience the whole series of lectures, not .any single lecture, which would only be like a ,broken pot to the whole of the vessel. (Hear, hear.) —Professor DAWKINS said he was present at that evening on the part of the Victoria University, the 'youngest university so far as he koew in the world, to show them that they were not unmindful of /heir duties in that part of England, so far as re- littedto University Extension. They knew that at the present time Oxford and Cambridge, and other -centres, were taking the liveliest interest in higher education outside their limited centre, and it seemed to them in Manchester that they could hardly fulfil their duties in that great district of lancaShire and Cheshire unless they instituted some system of the kind. He, therefore, was present that evening to put before 'them as plainly, and as simply as he could, a chapter out of the history of the world. He wanted to give them an idea of what geological methods really were, and he did not wish in the coursetf his remarks to use any long words or to use any technical language which he could avoid. As a matter of fact, he entirely agreed with his friend Professor Freeman, who told him that when- ever he knew a thing very well and wanted other people-to know it equally well he used short words; but 'whenever he did not know a thing very well or when he did not want other people to know what he meant he used long words. (Laughter.) That was to be the principle which he hoped would guide him through those lectures, and the long words 'he -would occasionally have to use must be put down not to his account but to the account of those unfortunate people who would have to suffer for their coinage in, perhaps, another world. (Laughter.) First of all, then, let him point out to them the line of inquiry he proposed to take. He was going to draw their attention to the ancient geography and geological history of Britain. He proposed to place before them as plainly as he could those changes by which Britain became what it is. All, or most Of them, had read "The Making of England," by his friend, John Richard Green. He proposed to plae..e before them a making which was far before the making of England. He proposed to place be- fore them the making of the British Isles. In dealing with that exceedingly interesting geo- graphical question he should take the opportunity of giving them, as far as he could, the principles which guided them in their inquiries into the an- cienthistory of the world; in other words, in their inquiries into geological matters. In first place, let him ask their attention to the method of their inquiry. In dealing with geology they were guided simply by the consideration of those causes which are in operation at the present time, in other words they looked around upon all those various operations which are going on at the present time on the surface of the earth, and they. saw whether, by means of an examination into their results, they could not read the story of the world as it is writ- ten in the great stone book of Nature. Present causes and present results were their guides in dealing with those facts. They must however, not forget that it was very possible, and indeed almost certain that in ancient times, when the world was young causes were much swifter in their operations than at present, simply because the earth was hotter. The lecturer then proceeded to show how the surface of the earth was affected by the action of the sea waves, by the fall of rain and flow of streams and rivers. Mountains, he said, were merely portions of the earth's surface which had been spared by the torrents and they stood out in relief. They had been chiselled out by the action of the tor- rents, and stood out for the same reason that the relief in the carved leg of a table stood out—because the rest of the material had been cut away. The action of ice and heat was also referred to as agents in the shaping of the earth's surface. In conclusion he said that the question of the whole geographrof this country was one of those things about which unfortunately he knew of no text book to which he could refer them. The gradual building up of Britain was comparatively a new subject.—The proceedings then concluded.

In Kimbolton Parish Church, on Saturday, Thomas Chattel', aged about 44, clerk of the parish, was dis- covered by his wife in a pew with his throat cut. He was quite dead. The efforts at the Landore Siernen's Steel Works, Wales, to avert a strike have proved fruitless, and the works were closed on Saturday. Two thousand men are thrown out of employment.

- - A large distillery at Fettereairn. Kincardineshire, was destrlyed by fire on Saturday night. About 1,000 quar- ters of barley and 300 casks of whisky were consumed, and the loss is said to be £20,000.

The Church Missionary Society has been the recipient of another handsome anonymous donati4 D. The gift is one of £5,500, and is to be applied to strengthening the Japan and Punjab mission of the society. An 11-ton howitzer gun, when being fired at the range of Ikon. Armstrong, Mitchell, and CO., at Silloth, on Saturday, burst, the breech and baSO part of the gun being blown out. Five persons were seriously injured. The Mayor of Bristol has reported that £2,000 of the city's Jubilee Fund has been sent to the Imperial Insti- tute, £2,600 has been spent in treats to the aged poor and children, and £1,300 was left towards providing a statue of the Queen. . DEATH OF THIS CHAMPION BLINDFOLD DRAUGHTS PLAYER. —We regret to record the death of Mr. William Strickland, the champion blindfold draughts player, which took place on Saturday morning after eleven days' illness. fro bronchitis. The deceased gentlemab, a Leeds man, came into prominence twenty-two years ago, when six- teen years of age. At the Thames Police Court, on Monday, Thos. Z. Barnes. aged 47, photographer, was charged with causing the death of his wife, by shooting her with a revolver, on the evening of last Saturday week, the revolver having been won in a raffle. The magistrate said he thought there was a doubt whether a jury -would convict., and he therefore discharged the prisoner.

A labourer in a state of helplcss drunkenness, while on his way from Tredegar to Dowlais, on Saturday night. laid down on the railway metals. and an engine coming up took off one of his boots and part of his foot. He told the engine-driver who came to him to mind his own business, and did not knew that he had been injured. An empty whisky bottle was found in his pocket Liverpool and district were on Monday enveloped in a dense fog, impeding railway and river traffic. Not- withstanding the use of bells and fog horns on the river, which were continuously sounded, the quarter to eight ferry boat, Claughton, collided with her consort,'the Lan- cashire, damaging the latter's paddle-box. Towards 11 o'clock the fog lifted, and bright sunshine followed. • •

The dead body of James Connelly. a labourer on the Forth Bridge Works, was found in Inverkeithing harbour on Sunday, having been terribly knocked about. It ap- pears that Connelly and some fellow-labourers quarrelled on Saturday night, having been previously drinking 'heavily, and four of the labourers lave accordingly been arrested on suspicion of killing the deceased.

Joseph Morley, aged 17, was again brought up at the Stratford Sessions, on Saturday, on the charge of mur- dering Martha Bod,ger, at Chigwell, on Tuesday last. The court was densely crowded. When the accused reached the court, a large crowd endeavoured to get. at him. As soon as the prisoner was put in the dock, In- vector Cudmore, of Woodford, asked for a remand, which was granted. —On Saturday last, the

THE Masmnaaran -- rday occasion of a grand bicycle and tricycle tournament. and the last day of the engagement of the famous band of the Royal' Artillery (Woolwich), the Exhibition was attended by the largest number which had hitherto passed the turnstiles in one day, 74,595 persons being registered, as against 70,141 on Jubilee Day. The total number of admissions, including Saturday, are 3,924,798. SERIOUS RESULT OF RwirLESS DaiviNO.—A trap acci- dent attended with serious consequences took place at Greenwich on Saturday morning. A man named Hen- derson, in an intoxicated condition, was driving a light trap towards East Greenwich, when, owing to the man- ner in which the horse was treated, it became unmanage- able, and dashed up the road at a furious speed, and before it could be pulled up ran into a brougham containing two ladies and three children. Henderson's horse was dreadfully injured, the pole of the brougham running into its chest, and the animal was instantly killed. Henderson was shockingly cut about the held, and his ribs were smashed. The driver and the brougham were uninjured, but both ladies were severely shaken. Tun Etkno SIIIRLD.—On Saturday evening the Duke of Cambridge was one of the guests of .the Lord Mayor on the occasion of a banquet given in celebration of the placing in the Guildhall of the Elcho Shield and the National Challenge Trophy won by the English Eight at Wimbledon. His Royal Highness, in responding to the toast of "The Army and Reserve Forces," said that hav- ing lately been in different parts of the country to examine the condition of the various arms of the ser- vice, he bad pleasure in stating that he found everything in so efficient a condition that they might he relied upon wherever they were sen't to maintain the high standard of former day& Thera was-no fear of conscription in this country, because in the volunteer force we had the finest conaeription in the-world. EXTRAORDINARY FRAUDS ON A BUILDING SOCIETY. -- The official report of the accountants engaged to in- vestigate the affairs of the Hull and Holderness Conser- vative Permanent Building Society, indicates that the total amount of the defalcations of the late secretary, Mr. R. Collison, whose suicide has already been reported, will amount ,to £21,000. In view of the loss of a sum of this magnitude, it is stated that the directors will in due course take proceedings to obtain a winding up order. The effects of the defalcations are far-reach- mg, and instances are being multiplied daily in which it is stated that much distress is being suffered through the frauds. It is also stated that all who remain on the list as sureties for the due performance of the society's engagements have been served with notices for the pay- ment of £2,000, the amount of their bonds. In one case this procedure must result in very great hardship'. In the firat year of the society's inception a gentleman, well known in Hull and district, became one of the sureties, but for several years past lw has ceased to have any connection with the undertaking. Unfortunately, as it now turns out, he neglected to take steps to have his bond cancelled, and remained on the list, and still incurred a responsibility which he imagined had ter- minated. TEE MYSTERIOUS DROwNino CA.SE AT BRADFORD.—On Saturday Charlotte Come (net Cohen, as previously stated), aged 17, domestic servant, who was rescued from the canal early on Friday morning, was.brought up at the police court on a charge of attemptin<, to commit suicide. It was stated by the Chief Constable that there was no foundation for the statement She made shortly after her rescue that she end the deceased, Sarah Simp- son, had been pushed into the canal. Letters had been found at their lodgings showing that they had arranged to drown themselves together, because they were out of situations and were without money. There was also reason to believe that tte deceased, who was 24 years of age, and had got into disgrace, had induced the prisoner to jump into the water 'with her. The prisoner WAS re- manded, being liberated in her own recognisance of £2O, conditional upon her placing herself in the meantime ander the care of the Discharged Pri'soners' Aid Society. —The inquest on the body of Sarah Simpson' was concluded at Bradford on Monday. The jury found that the deceased and her rescued friend,- Charlotte 'Come, domestic servant, had mutually agreed to commit suicide. The Coroner said this amounted to a verdict of wilful murder against the rescued person, and the jury r&ommended her to mercy on account of her youth. A warrant was issued for the arrest of Come. SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A DAIRY FARMER REMARK- ABLE RESUET.—A case was investigated at Chaster Castle. on Saturday, in which Arthur Ilandley, of Stamford Heath Farm, WIIS charged by the Cheshire Lines Com- mittee with under declaring the quantity of milk sent by him on six separate occasions from Mickle Trafford station to the Central station, Manchester. Mr. H. Hawkins, of Manchester, who prosecuted on behalf , o.f the railway company, said this was a very flagrant case indeed, for he would show that on the six days In question the defendant had under declared the quantity of the milk to the extent of Hila gallons. Evi- dence was called to bear out this statement. Anthony Bellwood, proprietor of the Manchester Creamery, Lower Broughton-road, Manchester, one of the witnesses called by the railway company, admitted in cross- examination that defendant, under a contract, sup- plied him with milk at 6id. a gallon. which was sold in the Exhibition at 2d. a glass !—For the defence, Mr. Churton said it was obligatory on a railway company, before securing a conviction, to conspicuously publish the particulars of the several offences and penalties under the Act of Parliament in the chief place of business of - the company, and, wherever the regulations were of local application, at local places too. This had not been done at Mekle Trafford Station, and the omission was fatal to the ease for the prosecution.—Mr. Hawkins, while admitting that he was taken by surprise, held that the section quoted applied only to offences under the by- laws and to frauds.—The magistrates said they felt themselves bound to dismiss the case on the technical noint " Catoao-Lrasann" Cough Lozenges, post free, 7d. Hay Bros., Id., Stockport.—Advt. JUBILEE CELEBRATION AT STRATFORD-ON-AVON. Stratford-on-Avon was ea fete on Monday morning, the occasion being the inauguration of a splendid drinking fountain presented to the town as a Jubilee memorial of the Queen's reign by Mr. G. W. Childs, of Philadelphia, the donor of the American window, Westminster Abbey. The ancient borough accepted the gift with enthusiasm, aod the Mayor and Corporation issued invitations to one hundred guests. The American Minister, Mr. Phelps, Sir Philip Cunliffe Owen, Lord Ronald Gower, and Mr. John Walter were the guests of the Mayor Sir Arthur Hodgson, Sir Cunliffe Owen, and Mr. Walter being per- sonal friends of Mr. Childs. Mr. Irving made the dedi- cation. He spoke of Mr. Childs as not only an admirable representative of the public spirit and enterprising energy of Philadelphia, but also as a man who has en- deared himself to a very wide circle by many generous deeds. After the ceremony the Mayor entertained the guests at luncheon. THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 22, 1887. - THE National Liberal Federation held its anJ anal meeting at Nottingham, on Tuesday, and' Proved to be one of the most successful demonstra- tions ever held by the Liberal party. There were over 2,200 delegates present from all parts of the country, and from the spirited addresses whicli werie delivered it was evident the speakers were ii good heart, and true to the core in their loyalty Ite Mr. GLADSTONE. Indeed, now that the Dissen- tient Liberals have separated from the main body, there is reason to believe that the Liberal party Will show itself more resolute and active in grap- Piing with the problems ot the hour. The Dissen- tients are, for the most part, of a Whiggish type; they have a liking for caves, and, like the original cave-dwellers, they are not men to advocate or hold by advanced ideas in methods of governmeot. Mr. GLADSTONE frankly acknowledged that what had happened had been extremely favourable to the interests of Liberalism, and even Radicalism; and this being so we may well be content, since the pace is accelerated, to have got rid of a bur- ' -den. There are some amongst the Dissentients whotmust feel that they are left in a very queer 'aorner ; and if they will only have the sense to Pull themselves together and make a move in the Tight direction, they may yet find themselves laurelling side by side with the rest of the Liberal Party. Mr. Wircrerrearnam and Mr. Bye it 4re taking this course; and more than this—to his honour, be if said—Mr. EVELYN, a Tory who irrlows what it is to keep a conscience, has intima- ted to his Deptford constituents that he will resign rather than be party to such a system of coercion aa that which has resulted in the butchery at Miti ll.elstown. The plain fact is that the Dissentient I Liberals are decreasing alike in influence and in aumbers, while on the other hand the Liberal Party is gaining strength every day. As to the liory Government, it is gradually sinking, as so Tautly Governments have sunk, in the quagmire of Coercion; but having commenced te by expres- ag its disapproval of a repressive, policy it will Pass out of existence "unwept, unhonoured, and llnsung." Lord Sthassratx was in his right 'ad when he said, two years ago, that such a coercive policy as was involved ,in the the renewal of the Crimes Act would create ten tikes as much mischief as it would repress. He I had turned his back then upon coercion, as he thought for ever, but having no policy of his own, %a, d being incapable of governing Ireland in a iititimate way, he has been led to resort to the 0141 bad method, with the result that—in harmony With his prediction—the? evil he is doing is ten tjui.. es as great as the evil he can put down. When liord SALISBURY came into office, Ireland was hopeful and peaceful; now, whipped by the scorpion clif _coercion, she is crying aloud in her misery, and 14 on the verge of revolt. The Government talk %Out upllolding the law, but, as Mr. GLADSTONE showed in his speech on Tuesday, they are them- eclves the.violators of the law. .They are trying l° strangle a free press, and to trample on the right 5f free speech. But the public feeling is too 4ttlorig for them; and their base weapons are 'leaking in their hands. The present Ministry Itre noi a Government; they are marauders who L°Tarnit their depredations fir the name of the law. „t'illa violence of their policy is equalled only, as GrAnsrorre remarks, by its impotence. And .46-S is why it cannot last. It is derided by those Who would support it if the Government were Bhtrculg enough to make a wilderness and call it ''`lf-s,e• Its own followera are falling away from ; the nation is ready to shake it off when the °PPertunity arrives; and there is a growing feeling hich the meeting of Tuesday will strengthen— wlat the opportunity cannot be far away.

4 .The question of Making the Warrington Library ,free Lending Libr.ry, "as is the case in the sur: ' v—uni ding towns of Wigan, St. Helens, Runcorn, ,n 1 es, and over one hundred other towns in the ted Kingdom," will come before the Town '7'1161 on Tuesday next for discussion and deci- ton • Councillor Wirzum PIBBPOINT gave notice,

immediately after the last meeting, of a resolution to the effect that the Town Council should appoint a Special Committee to take the whole question into consideration, and to report thereon. Mean- time, the Library and Museuni Committee have again had the matter under crideration, and the only proposal, we understand, they have to make is that, in addition to continuing the present form of subscription, readers who cannot afford to pay quarterly or yearly, shall be charged one penny for every book borrowed. This would, of course, make payment easier, but, unfortunately, it does not touch the real question at issue. The demand made is 'or a Free Lending Library—not for one at which the subscription is at the rate of one penny per book, or five shillings per year. If the gentlemen who constitute the Library Committee were the repre- sentatives of a private institution it would be per- fectly legitimate on their part to make these regu- lations as to charges—just as it used to be the case with the medicine dispensed at the Infirmary. But the difference is that they are dealing with a pub- lic institution—with an institution belonging to the ratepayers-.--and that • they have no right to dole out books and charge for them ai.though they were doses of medicine. The penny in the pound for the support of the Library and Museum is taken from the ratepayers compulsorily, but it is taken from them on the distinct understanding that the privileges of the institutions are "free of all charge." If it were not so, the law would be a mockery, a delusion, and a snare. Throughout
the country the inhabitants of the various towns

under the Libraries Acts have cheerfully paid their penny in the pound for the support' of Libraries and Museums; but it has been because they believed they were to have Free Libraries. They would have opposed the rate, as they would be justified in opposing it, had they been told that, before they could take al book home to read, they would be called upon to pay such a sum by way of a second tax, as the Committee might determine. Is it not absurd, on the face of it, to suppose that the Legislature would carefully fix the exact charge—a penny in the pound —and then leave it to a Committee to' charge anything additional they might think fit? The fact is, the Committee have no more right to demand a subscription, large or small, after the rate has been paid than • they have to insist on an extra shilling after the poor's rate has been paid. They may receive subscriptions or donations, but-they cannot legally give any privilege to one ratepayer over another in consequence of those subscriptions or donations. If there was ever any doubt On the subject that was set at rest by the ATTORNEY- GENERAL, when, in answer to ? question put by Mr. BRADLAUGH in the House of Commons, he said :—" There is no authority under the Libra- ries Act of 1855 for making any distinction be- tween persons who subscribe and persons who do not." In other words, the person who subscribes can have no privilege under the Act to which a person who does not subscribe is not equally en- titled. This is sound law and sound sense, and the sooner it is acknowledged and put in practice, as it is in other towns, the sooner willWarrington deal justly with its inhabitants, an& take away the reproach which attaches to it by supporting a Free Library which is not free. Since the above was put in type, we have re- ceived a copy of the report of the Library Sub- Committee which seems to call for a few lines of comment, seeing that it will come before the Town Council, on Tuesday: It is especially signi- ficant that the report expresses no opinion as to whether it is legal to make a charge. And yet this is the primary issue. If the committee cam show that the ltaw authorises a charge let them do so, and the agitation for a Free Lending Library will terminate. If they cannot show this—if tlie com- mittee are breaking the law—is it not time that the whole question was gone into by the Town Council itself? We are told that "the Acts of Parliament do not require the ',establishment of a Free Lending Library;" but our point is that hav- ing established a Lending Library under the Acts, it must be free to the ratepayers. If the Acts- give authority to establish a Subscription Library, why do they not quote the section The case of Wigan is cited for comparison; but if the Warrington Corporation will do as Wigan has done irr two particulars only they may make the Library a Free Lending Library next week. To be on a foot- ing with Wigan is what the ratepayers demand. For instance, we learn that, at Wigan, the Cbr- poration do not charge for gas and coke, which saves as much as £B4 per year: Then they have levied a Voluntary Rate, which• last year produced 1.41. If Warrington took the same course, the saving in gas and coke would be £76, and if—assuming War- rington was less liberal than Wigan—a voluntary rate brought in £lOO only, there would still be, a total gain to 'the Library Committee of £37,13, which is more than the whole sum received from subscriptions. The Committee thus stand con- victed by their own report. They cite Wigan, and we ask them to follow the example a Wigan— cease to charge for gas and coke, levy a Voluntary rate, and make the Library a Free Lending Library.

There was a Conference of Co-operative dele- gates at Hebden Bridge, on Saturday, which is likely to lead to important results. Lord RIPON presided, and several representative men were present and took part in the discussion, including Ma. E. V. NEALE, the general secretary, and MR. GEORGE JACOB "HOLYOAKE. MR. NEALE seems to think' the time has come when Co-opera- tors should hark back to their original views, and take steps for providing that the workers, as well as the money finders, shall share the profits. This principle, it is held, should apply to productive industries, and the main difficulty at present is that the various Co-operative Societies are, for the most part, engaged in the work of distribution rather than of production. There has been a great success with "stores "—that is with the machinery provided for the distribution of goods —but in the matter of manufacture the application of the principle of co-operative effort has been less successful. Can it be that this is because the worker has not been taken into ac- count when profits had to be shared? Mr. HOLYOAKE would answer in the affirmative, for he says :—" Under this system there would be fer- tility of invention, fidelity of work, interest in the concern, and animation throughout, with pride in all the operations of the productive society, and the profits that the co-operators had made in their stores would be insignificant compared with the opulence of gain which would accrue when every store had its productive workshop." This is a glowing picture of what might be expected when the workman is allowed to participate in the ire- suit, and if it proved to be only half true it would effect a revolution of the most momentous kind. What is required is to get a large body of capi- talists to give the experiment a fair trial. Several co-operative societies have experimented with bene- ficial results, the profits amounting to as much as fifteen per cent. • workpeople to share the profits. Besides, as is always Urged, there are losses as well as profits, and those who share the one should share the other. Still, this objection could be met by setting aside, in the first instance, a substantial sum from the first gains as a Reserve Fund to be made use of for meeting losses. It would be comparatively easy to make the trial with Co- operative Companies, for their business in all its features is known to the members to begin with, and they are accustomed to a Reserve Fund for various purposes. We can imagine the money finders saying that those who want profits should find funds. But, on the other hand, it might be suggested even to the men who are greedy of gain that they would be more likely by this system to to have an unfailing profit than by any other. Lord Rirozi. showed himself favourable to 'the pro- posal; for he remarked that the worker in any co-operative undertaking had a claim bn the re- sults prior to that of the purchaser or the consu- mer. But he did not counsel any hasty decision; "he believed what was required at this momen was that the subject should be thoroughly threshed out." We quite agreg with him, and trust that co-operators throughout the kingdom will give the matter immediate attention. At the present moment the social problem presses more and more upon the community. What a blessing It would be if it could be solved by co-operative profit sharing between capital and labour.

A BUTCHER'S TROUBLES MU WIDNES : HEAVY' rfNE.— .At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursdayi•before Mr. F. If. Gossage and Mr. T. S.l Timmis, George. Davidson, i'butcher, Anne-street, was ,charged with, having on his premises the lung and melt of a boast, wfoich was diseased and unfit for human food, in the course of pre- paration for sale. Mr. Jr T. Allen prosecuted on behalf of the Local Board, and Mr. J. W. Knowles defended. Mr. John Dickson, sanitary inspector, said he visited the defendant's premises on the 16th Sbptember. He found the lung and melt of cebeast in a state‘of decomposition. The meat was condemned by a• veterinary. surgeon and by the magistrates, and was destroyed.—ln cross-exam- ination, Mr. Dickson. said the meat was worth about 2d, but very much mornwhen manufactured. He could not see that the meat was bad untithe cut into it. He knew that the defendant had arranged to dispose of his busi- ness on the Ist November.—)r: Knowles said Davidson commenced business seven years ago, and after twelve months had elapsed he was fined- £5 for having bad ment in his possession. ThrougAo this injury to his reputation he had to give up business, and he resorted to his former occupation of chemical bobourer. Two years and a half ago he again commenced' business, but a second convic- tion and fine of £5 being recorded against him his busi- ness was practically ruined, At present he W 196: over head and ears in debt, he had a wife who was at present very ill, and foin children. to maintain, and Mr. Knowles asked for mercy on these grounds. General Boulanger admits that his mother was a Welsh woman, and states that her name was Griffith. Well done little Wales! Mr. H. M. Stanley is a Welshman, and, and—wasn't John Milton a Welsh poet?

• It is reported from Fredensberg that the Grand Duke Mithael has "caught the measles." This may be thought very clever of his Russian Highness, but in Vngland even the children can catch measles—or &cold.

A Warrington puddler named Stokes hash been trying to "shoot the rnoon "—that is t& say he has been removing his goods before paying his rent. His little escapade has ended in hiabeing brought before the magistnates, and, as they have ordered him to pay the rent and pay costs*it is thought he will aim at lower game next time.

1; At Huyton, on Tuesday,, a labourer named 10'W-1m was sent to gaol for stealing—above all !ithing—two prayer books fmm two Catholic i Chapels. So determined was he to be godly•that, betstole the ?mans of grace. It is to be hoped that hes 7:1!;, not past praying for, and that he will buy theinext book he takes a fancy to;. and turn over Air nevo-lisaf.

Who, is, to be Mayor of Warrington foi theft next year?' The Tories will say a Liberal is out of the question ; and they are turning over the names of Alderman Sutton, Councillor John Pier- point, andiCouncillor Francomb. There are some who think: Alderman Pickmere should .be asked again. Tha6would be a great compliment to him; but wouldit be complimentary to theiCorporation as a whole ?- It would seem as if the Tories were played out, lit they compelled his worship to be- come Mayorffor the sixth time.

A boatmarnat Runcorn was broughtbefore the magistrates on Monday for having assaulted a woman.. It was stated that the poor creature was found,firthe street crying, her clothebtorn, and her face covered with blood. When spoYten to, the ruffian threatened to murder her. After hearink of all this, the bench fined him ss. and mats But the explanation is simple—the woman, was his wife. And what is the use of having a wife, if a fellow cannot half murder her at the rate of ss. and costs

The National 'Liberal Federation is goirskahead ; it is Liberal. PA has laid down as one plank in its platform immediate reform in registration law on the basis of "one man one vote." Next.to this we have the diSestablishraent of the English Church in Wales. This will, of course, rouse the ire of Church-people who have not yet cat their wisdom teeth, and we shall hear the changes rung, as heretofOre, on " spoliation," "robbery," "dese- cration," &C., &e.,

But thisis not all; there is more and yet more. The Association is in favour of local option, land law reform, local government reform, and free ,education. There, now, you Reformers,. fel not that enough to make your mouths water ? It is something tb lookforward to; something tb'work for when the Irish question is settled. But that of course first. "Ireland blocks the wan? but there are signs that this will be removed before long. The block iS so bad that it moat be removed. ,

Mr. Geschen made a speech at, Bradford on Tuesday evenin,p,and in the course of it he ven- tured to appeal to 'the democracy. How envious! Mr. Goschen appealed some time ago to the democracy. of Edinburgh and Liverpool, and was despised and rejected by them. But the demo- cracy Of Ehgland' is 'responding to the appeal of the Irish democracy; they see that the Goschens and thesßalfounr are resorting to, bludgeons and bayonets; but they can still say, in the words of Byron—
Yet freedom, yet thy banner torn but flying, Streams Elms, thunder-cloud against the wind.

Another accident with a paraffin. hump. This time the victim is a woman, living t Garston, named Mrs. Dunbavin. She let the lamp fall, set fire to her clothes, and was almost burnt to death. So many lives are lost through•the use of defective lamps that it is a fair question whether a law should not be passed prohibiting the sale of any but safety lamps. A safety lamp does not cost much more than one which, from its ravages, might be called the death-dealer.

A. curious story comes from Ireland of a cure for hydrophobia which is said to be made use of with unvarying success by a family named the 141T4overns. They want to sell the secret, as they are poor, but of "kingly origin." We are told that:—" The beautiful round full eye grey or brown; the auburn hair tending to golden; the kingly front and the perfect symmetry of form characterise this remarkable race." This is very pretty, and if it is not tan Irish romance the secret of the M`Governs should be obtained at any cost.

There is an old saying that you can be married in Scotland by hopping over a broomstick. It is not quite as bad as that, but nearly. .A young lady named Livesey went through a form of betrothal with a man named Harvey, and found afterwards that she was really married to the man, although they never lived together. She could hardly be called a wife, and yet she has had to apply for a divorce, which she has succeeded in obtaining. Some fine day when Parliament has got through bigger jobs, it will be urged to turn its attention to the marriage law.
John Smith, farmer, of Parr, has been fined 40s, and costs for depositing a caroms for sale at Liver.

The librarian reported that during the month 1,780 volumes had beenisaued from the library. ACCIDENT AT WIDNES,—Peter Riley, a married man, who resides at 23, Pear-street, was seriously injured, .on Sunday, whilst following his employment at the 'works of Messrs. Golding, Davis, and Col: Through fiOnin Un- explained cause the lid of a caustre pot fell upon his leg andseverely crushed the limb, which was afterwards dressed by Dr. UutchinSon. . _

—,iiSl-170E; TO BLACKPOOL should stay at the Station Temper- ance Hotel, right opposite Central Statilin. Central position. Commodious and accommodating. Terms easy.—Apply J: Heap.—Advt. Ting REV. E. JONES, Welsh Presbyterian Minister, of Runcorn and Widnes, died on Saturday morning, after a' brief illness. The deceased, who has laboured in the ^ district for four years, Wits a talented preacher in the Welsh vernacular, and also a fair English preacher. The funeral took place on Tuesday, and was attended by the Nonconformist ministers of Runcorn. WIDNES GYMNASIUM HARRIERS.—The members of this club had a really enjoyable run on Saturday. Starting from the Millfield Inn, Appleton,•at 3-30',.they proceeded to Upton Rocks, and from there toßainbiil by Crondm. A slight rest was indulged in there, and the party then proceeded towards home at a smart pace. -Etheridge was first home, after a smart finish with McMahon, Cowley, Fescoe, and Franklin being next, the ethers ^ following indiscriminately.

PRIMFFIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, FRODSIILM BRIDGE.— On Sunday harvest thanksgiving services were conduc- ted in this place of worship. The• liberal contributions 'ofTruit, &c., Were well arranged, and gave a pleasing aspect to the building. There were some very pretty de- viees formed of wheat and oats, by Mr. Yarwood, of Sutton Bridge. Mr. Webb, of Preston Brook, presided at the hairrnonimn, and appropriate anthems werewell rendered bye choir of friends from adjacent villages. The con- gregatiorer were good. SHOCKING PARAFFIN LAMP ACCIDENT AIF GARSTON.— About eleven o'clock last night, two married women, named' Dunbavin and Heaps, who live in Wood-street, Garston, went to visit a friend, Mrs. Slaterr.of 3, Court, Woo/ton-road, Garston. They found her in bed, there-' fore-Mrs. Dunbavin took the lamp off the table, and fol- lowed by Mrs. Heaps was proceeding upstairs, when she let the lamp fall on her. It set fire to her clothes, which in a; moment were one mass of flames. The poor women screamed for assistance, arid Police-sergeant Devonport, wheehappened tobe passing, ran into her assistance and bywrapping clothing, &c., round hermanaged tosubdue the,fl'annes. The woman ,Was fearfully burnt all over the body, and on the advice df Dr. Fisher, who was called in to attend her, she was removed to the local hccident hos- pital; where she now lies in a very dangerous condition. Mil'. Heaps was also very badly burnt. WRYER'S LACROSSE V. LIVERPOOL (2).—This match was played at Hough Green on Saturday, and' resulted in a victory for the home team by 4 goals to 3. Widnes suf- fered from the absence of two of their best attacks, which caused a rearrangement of the team, and spoiled their combination, which is so essential tasuccess in the game. Two thirties were played. Widnes, losing the toss, had, to play uphill, hut with the sun- and wind in their favour. The home team immediately began to attack the Liverpool goal, but were prevented from scoring for some time by the good defence-of Boumphrey and Miller in goal. At length J. Wylde shot the ball through, G. Halsall following suit soon' after. Before half time, H. S. Gossage had added a third-goal to the score, which, at the interval, stood at 3'to 0 in favour of the home team. After half time the game was more equal; in fact, Liverpool scored 3 goals to Widnes 1 (cileasage). A pleasant game ended, as stated above, in a win,for the home team. This was the- first match of the Widnes season, and no doubt they will be able to show a good proportion of wins at the- close of their lengthy list of fixtures, which includes matches with tho &A teams of such well-known clubs as Liverpool, , Cheadle, Stockport, Didsbury, &c. RUNCORN DAUGHTERS OF Temesaasice.—On Monday evening the Daughters of Temperance held a conversa- zione in the Regent-street Schoolroom, and the proceed- ings were of a very interesting character. There was a good attendance. Mr. J. W. Woodland presided, and in a neat interesting address, spoke of the advantages of total abstinence, and highly eulogised' the Daughters of Temperance Order. A most interesting programme was then gone through, consisting of songs. glees, trios, read- ings, and recitations rendered by the following ladies and gentlemen :—Misses Kersley, Rogers, Woodward, and Kniveton ; Messrs. S. Ba.zley, C. Leathwood, A. Stubbs, W. Tickle, J. T. Holt, and Boyle. Miss Tem- perley was the accompanist. During the evening Mr. Thomas Cooke gave an encouraging report of the order, and spoke of the advantages to be derived by joining the Daughters of Temperance, urging upon the ladies present to connect themselves with such an organisation. He stated that during the year 99 ladies had joined the order making their number now- 595, with a cash bal- ance in hand of nearly £6OO. Alluding to the longevity of the members of the order, Mr. Cooke mentioned the death rate for the year only being two per 1,000, whilst their sick rate had only been 64 days per member. The first part of the programme having been gone through, refreshments of a varied kind were then handed round, including fruit and sweetmeats of various sorts. After- wards games of an enjoyable nature were heartily joined in by all present-, and a most pleasant evening was spent. HALTON PARISH CHITRCII HARVEST FESTIVAL. The annual services of thanksgiving for the abundant har- vest were commenced at Halton Parish Church on Fri. day evening last week. The customary taste and skill had been displayed iti the elaborate decorations, and the, sacred edifice presented an appearance that was charm- ing in the extreme. Lady Brooke, assisted by the mem- bers of her family, undertook the work of adorning the chancel, according to her usual custom, and the result I was an exquisite arrangement of choice fruits, flowers,. and cereals, which excited the admiration of the many hundreds who attended the services. The following were also decorated with artistic skill :—pulpit, Mrs. T. Wright; reading desk, Mrs. Joseph Stokes; the font, Mrs. J. W. Haddock; and other parts were decorated by Mrs. Henry Dale and Mrs. Hamblett ; Misses Wilson, Hamblett, Lambert, Baiplley, Wright, Ackerley, Wbodier Jeacock, Jones, Chrime,s, Forster Povey,, Dale, and Johnson, together with a number of gentlemen. Mate- riaN fin- decorative purposes were kindly contributed by Sir Richard and Lady Brooke. of Norton Priory ;Messrs. T. Stokes, T. Wright (churchwardens)', J. W'. Baguley, Johnston, Henry Dale, Vr. Nixon, Rutter, Aekerley, Baker (Clifton Hall), John Finch (Astraoor),. Woodward, Miss Leach, Mesdames J. W. Haddock, Perry, John Tomlinson, Astburyt &a. A large congregation assem- bled on Friday evening, when the Rev-. the Earl of Mul- , grave, M.A. (vicar of Worsley) was the preacher, and delivered a sermon from the words "Breed enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger," Luke xv, part of the 17th verse. The choir sang anthems and specially selected hymns in a` very creditable style. Mr. Jeacock presided at the organ. The services were continued on Sunday, when the Rev. G. Bartle, D.D.,'D.C.L., princi- pal of Wellesley College, Southport, occupied the pulpit both morning and evening. In the afternoon the Rev. W. Fielding, 8.A., curate of Aston, conducted a service. The sacred edifice was crowded In the evening and seve- ral hundrects were unable to gain admittance. Collee- tions were taken in aid of the Church Improvemertt Fund and other objects._

div.p: AN UNIVERSAL AVALANCHE.
THOUSANDS OF PEOPLE CRUSHED BY ITS PITILESS POWER.

Far up the dizzy Alpine heights, above the itne of perpetual frost, where the brilliant glitter of the snow under the midday sun seems only to inten- sify the cold, the Ice King would seem to hold un disputed sway. But even here there is at times a little humidity in the atmosphere of the more shel- tered nooks, The dry snow softens a little, the wind catches it up and tosses it about, and the stat-like flakes are rolled into a tiny ball that the footsteps of a child might easily I crush. Then comes the rude blast from the mountain top, and drives the ball up and down the high valley and across the vast, trackless fields of snow and ice. It gathers size and strength at every turn; huge rocky boulders and mountains of ice are embedded in the now slowly moving avalanche which sooner or later descends with frightful velocity to the valley below. The luckless village in its pathway is doomed! The air is thick with the falling snow! An awful rush! A rear rev( rb irates through the mountains, and the little Swiss ha mlat is swept away! As the wind catches up the snow particles on the mountain tops, so the heart catches up the blood as it passes through the kidneys and other organs, and sends it coursing through the system. As it rushes along, it drops the uric acid that the unhealthy kidneys have left in the blood in the form of insoluble crystals, causing enlargement of the joints and intense inflammation in the system, which is often called acute rheumatism. Eventually the joints enlarged by these crystals become stiff and painful. If these crystals are dropped in the liver, they are called gall-stones; if in the kidneys, gravel; if in the bladder, calculas, or stone. If this uric acid, or kidney poison, remains in solution in the blood, it circulates throughout the system caus- ing irritation, which produces, according to the location of the irritation, pneumonia, consumption, hacking cough, heart disease, inflammation and fevers, skin dis- orders, paralysis, apoplexy, and makes the system sus- ceptible to colds, chills, and all the other common dis- orders of which uric acid is the principal cause. The little child upon the mountain top can crush in its tiny hand the first formation of the rushing ava- lanche. Soo, too, the calamitous results noted can be as readily .prevented if the right means are used at the right time. "But how?" our readers may ask. Listen, and we will tell you. It is a fact of medical science that the kidneys are the chief blood purifiers of the system; the chief blood poisoner is uric acid, which the kidneys alone can expel. If the thousand little hair- like sewer tubes of the kidneys—through which the en- tire blood supply passes, the same as through the heart— are diseased, they cannot separate and expel this poison- ous waste matter from the blood. Now, as another matter of scientific fact, disease of these little sewer tubes is more common than of any other delicate part of the body, and it is because War- ner's SAFE Cure, gentle and natural in its action, has such wonderful power in preventing and curing disease of these all-important tubes, that it is recognised as a great scientific specific—a power possessed by no other such remedy on earth. When the kidneys, the only blood-purifying organs, become inactive and diseased any disorder to which the system is most liable may be expected. Then it is that trouble begins, and the doctors fail mis- erably, because they can only treat the effects—the cause is beyond their power! Hence it is that the proprietors of Warner's SAFE CURE—which can be had of all chemists—claim to cure so many apparently different diseases; it, and it alone, reaches and cures the cause, and then, of course, the effects disappear: We incline to the belief that their theory is correct, and so recognised by scientists who have given the subject much study. This frightful disorder is depopulating our homes faster than we are aware of. Like the avalanche of the moun- tain, it is causing the death of all with whom it comes in contact. It does not sweep away an entire village or hamlet at once, but one by one the people succumb to its pitiless power. The final, or terminating cause may be given another name, and be so treated by various ex- perts," but the cause of all these effects, how many soever they may be, is the same, and for that cause there is but one rational form of treatment. If you do not crush the avalanche as it is forming, in the manner indicated, it will certainly crush you! Take your choice I.—England, Sept. 17.
