WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY. —Before the Mayor (Aldermaa Pi!...tmere), Alderman Harrison, and Ccouncillor LT'An Pierpoint. Derrantr.nmss.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence :=William Ward, in Buttermarket-street, on Sunday: night, fined ss, including costs; Thomas Crockan, in Wilderspool-road, on the same morning, fined ss, including costs; Edwin Thompson, in %nuts- ford-road, on the 6th just, fined Ss and costs; Daniel Hennessey, in Buttermarket-street, on the 9th lust, sent to prison for a month. DisTtramNci Tyre Pc.—Michael Daley, for commit- ting a breach of the peace by fighting in Buttermarket- street, was ordered to pay 4s 6d costs.—Elizabeth Pat- chett, who was charged with having been disorderly in the market, was dismissed.—John Mannion and Winifred Conway, 'charged with disturbing the peace by fighting in Winwiek-road, were dismissed with a caution. FTIRIODS DRIVING.—For having furiously driven a horse and cart in Bridge-street, on the 6th inst, Samuel Shaw was fined ss, including costs. BEGGING.—John Taylor, labourer, Bolton, was sent to prison for a month for vagrancy, he having been found guilty of begging in Winwick-street, on the 15th inst.— John McCormack, sailor, Dublin, was put in the dock on a similar charge, and was further charged with breaking a utensil at the Bridewell. He also was sent to prison for a month. ScHoot ATTENDANCE CASES.—The following were on the evidence of Mr. Riley, school attendance officer, fined Ss and costs for neglecting to send their children regularly to school :-7Patrick Lynch, forgeman, Gee-st. ; Walter Tolley, labourer, Bank Quay; John Lee, forge- man, Cockhedge ; William Lawrenson, wiredrawer, Dial-street; Cornelius Lennon, forgeman, Portland-st. ; Thomas Wright, glassmaker, Bank Quay; William Harding, wiredrawer, Orchard-street; Thomas Taylor, miller, Mersey Mills; and John Forster, alias John Rooney. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley and Mr. John

Fairclough. DRUNICENNRSS.—John Jordan was lined ss, including costs, for having been drunk and disorderly in Butter- market-street on the evening previous. Tasyr or A SHlRT.—Thomas Troy (18) and Catherine Maguire, a woman of about forty years of age, were charged with stealing, or receiving, knowing it to have been stolen, a shirt, the property of Luke Dermody, of 56, Tanners-lane. Mrs. Maguire, who had pawned the shirt at the request of the male prisoner, was discharged, and was then put in the witness box to give evidence against him.—Troy, who has previously been convicted of theft, was sentenced to three months' imprisonment, with hard labour. • -

Tlll7RSDAT.—Before Major Litton. THREATS.—James Whittaker, Wigan, was charged with having used malicious threats to a young woman named Alice Warburton, on the 9th inst. He was dis- missed on payment of the cost of the summons. FRlDAT.—Before Mr. John White (in the chair), Alder- man Harrison, and Dr. Gomall.

BaceatNo.-=Thomas Mo'oney, an elderly man, was charged with begging alms in Buttermarket-street, on the previous night. It appearing that he was of unsound mind, the Bench remanded him to the Workhouse.— John Robinson, whe• Was also charged with begging, was dismissed on promising to leave the town. DRUNKENNESS .—John Rice, for having been drunk and disorderly in Parker-street, on Thursday, was fined 10s and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment in default of pay- ment.—Jas. McCrow, for having been diunk and disorderly in Winwick-street, on the evening previous, was find ss, including costs, and a fustian cutter named Mary Jane Ellis, for haling been drunk in Irlam-street, on the pre- vious night, was fined Ss and costs. MAINTENANCE CASES.—Thomas O'Brien was committed to prison for 30 days for non-payment of arrears, amounting to £1 10s, under an order made upon him to contribute towards the support of his wife.—John Henry Charnock was ordered to pay Is 6d a week towards the support of his father, and George Charnock was ordered to pay is a week. • ASSAULT.—Hannah Webb, who was charged with hav- ing, on the 16th inst, assaulted Sarah Ann Barrett, was ordered to be bound over in her own recognisances to be of good behaviour, or go to prison for seven days.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—hefore Mr. Edward Green.all and Mr. R. Houghton. REFUSING TO Qurr.—Ed-ward Atherton, farm labourer, -was summoned for having been drunk on the licensed premises of Charles Petford, at Rixton-with-Glazebrook, on the 3rd inst., and for haying refused to quit when re- quested. He was fined Ss. and costs. DISTURBING 'ma PEACE.—William Wright, for creating a disturbance by fighting in the highway at Rixton-with- Glazebrook, on the 3rd inst., was bound over In his own racognisances of 2.5 to keep the peace for six months. A SLEEPY DRlVER.—Thornas Hankinson was fined ss, and costs for having been asleep while in charge of a horse and cart at Rixton-ivith-Glazebrook, on the 7th instant. DRUNKENNESB.—WiIIiam Holding, summoned for hav- ing been drunk and disorderly on the highway at Bur- ton-wood, on the 15th instant, was fined ss. and costs.— Patrick Mulroy, who was charged with having been drunk in Chapel-lane, Burtonwood, on the 16th instant, was fined 5€4. and costs.

OBSTRIICI7OI.7 K. B72.—Joseph Miller was sum- moned for having caused an obstruction in Warrington- road, Penketh, by allowing three horses and a 'bus to stand there for a period of twenty minutes on the Bth instant. Defendant said that it had been customary to allow the 'bus to stand there for half an hour every night for the last three years. The 'bus left Warrington at ten o'clock, arrived at Penketh half an hour later, and corn-
tnenced the return journey at eleven o'clock. The Bench ordered the defendant to pay the costs of the , case.
Frnnwonns.—William Whitfield, a lad, -was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for discharging fireworks on the highway, at Penketh, on the 11th inst. -
LYMM PETTY SESSIONS. Farnsir.—Before Messrs. P. Stubs, C. Lister, and H.
Stanton.

DRUNIEENNESS.—Mary Brazendale, drunk at Lymm. 10th Sept.; 58. and costs. DOGS AT LADGE.—Donald David, McPherson; John Scattergood, and. John Hatton, butcher, were each fined is. and costs for having allowed dogs to be at large, ALLEGED ASSIIILT.—Levi Bradburn was charged with having, on the 17th September, assaulted Hannah Antro- bus Maxwell, the wife of the instructor of the Lymm volunteers. Mrs. Maxwell stated that defendant's boy struck her sonlvith a whip, and when she ran out to where this happened the defendant put his hand in her face and threatened her. The case was dismissed. FIREWORICS.—Licenses for the sale of fireworks were granted to John Booth and Elizabeth Gibbon. A WITHDRAWAL.—Francis Whitlow was summoned for having assaulted an old man named Peter Leather, at Agden on the 20th September. A cross-summons had also been taken out. Mr. Fletcher, of Nortiswich, who appeared on behalf of Leather, asked to be allowed to withdraw the summons as, on being consulted, he had advised his client to take a civil action for compensation for the serious injuries he had sustained. Mr. A. Browne, of Warrington, appeared for Whitlow, and after having consulted his client he agreed to the withdrawal of both summonses. After some hesitation, the Bench allowed the summonses to be withdrawn.

div.p: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS._

MONDAY.—Before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Mr. James Handley. CELEBRATING A BIRTHDAY.—CharIes Rowles, aged 13, pleaded guilty to firing fireworks in Bridge-street on the 12th October. P.C. Millington proved the case, and said the boy threw the case into Mr. Johnson's shop.— The defendant denied throwing the exploded case into ' the shop. He and some other boys were celebrating a companion's birthday.—He was ordered to pay 3s. 6d. costs. REFUSING TO Qtnv.—David Taylor and Philip Taylor, brothers, were charged with having, on the 9th October, been drunk and disorderly in the Village Inn, Halton, and refused to quit when requested by the landlord, Charles Whitfield. The men entered the house at 20 minutes to ten at night, and, being drunk, the landlord declined to supply them with liquor. Their conduct afterwards was most violent and abusive. Philip did not appear, and a warrant was issued for his apprehension. David was fined 10s. and costs, Bs. 6d., or in default 14 days' hard labour. MISCELLANEOUS.—For allowing the chimney of his dwelling-house to be on fire, John Flannigan was fined 6d. and costs, Bs. 6d. Margaret Martin, Anthony Welsh, and John Doyle were each fined 10s. and costs for drunk and disorderly conduct. George Weldon' for begging in High-street, was on the evidence of P.C. Millington sen- tenced to seven days' hard labour. Foam= OnsTnucrioN.—Henry Salt, a boatman, pleaded guilty to having, oil the 2nd inst. obstructed the footpath in High-street.—P.S. Woolley narrated the cir- cumstances, and the prisoner was ordered toy 14s. 6d. —Superintendent Hollingsworth said he had received numerous complaints from the congregations of churches and chapels with regard to this nuisance, and in future he should ask that a heavy penalty be inflicted.—Mr. Reynolds said that was only reasonable. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE.—Jas. McTusk, a respectable _ . _ .

looking man, was charged with being drunk, and with conducting himself in an indecent manner. He was also charged with assaulting P.C. Millington.—When appre- hended on the first charge on Saturday night the pri- soner became very violent, and struck the officer several times.—A fine of 10s. and costs. Bs. 4d., was imposed for each offence.

DltuENNEss—Michael Quinn, Milton-street, Sarah Jones, Wigan, Edward Lacey, Clapgate, Wigan, were each fined ss. and costs for drunkenness. Catherine Carey, who made her 33rd appearance, was fined 100 and costs for a similar offence. _ . _

Sumencria Our.—Patrick McMahon, of no settled resi- dence, was sentenced to seven days' hard labour on a charge of sleeping in a chemical works.

Each defendant was bound over.—For allowing her horse to stray in Peelhouse-lane, Mary Murphy was fined is, and costs 7s. The Chairman said this was a dangerous practice, and offenders in future would be severely pun- ished.

WIDNES 'V. ASPULL.—These teams met at New Springs on Saturday, in the presence of about 1,500 spectators. This was the opening match of the new ground of the Aspull club, the removal to which from the more remote ground of last year has caused such trouble amongst the members, both playing and honorary, of this once rising dub; and the result—a victory of two goals and thaee minors against a try and five minors—was received with, the utmost satisfaction by their supporters. The Aspull team as it *ands at present, was fully represented, but Widnes was sends sorely by the absence of Par- kinson and Plumpton. Had they been playing in their usual form, it is not too much to say that 'Aspull would have beenscontent with playing second fiddle. It was about twenty minutes past four when the ball was put in motion. At once the Widnesians began the assault, 1 and in a couple of minutes had scored a minor. The kick out relieved the pressure, and then the home team took the ball to their opponents' line, and Seddon, who received the ball by a neat pass by Cartwright, dropped a fine goal. This put the Widnes men on their metal, and Farrell, who was the best back on the field, after a smart run secured a try. Kiddie failed to improve. Play for a long time was very keen and evenly contested, though Widnes, as their score of minors shows plainly, had some advantag,e, until their full back, S. Bingham, made a most serious mistake. He carried the ball in touch in his own quarter, and, though only one of his men was up as against at least ten of the home team, he threw the sphere to Fogg, but Dempsey got hold and had a clear course for a try. Pilkington landed a beautiful goal. Subsequently the Widriesians penned their oppo- nents to their line, but were unable to score anything more than a touchdown, though Farrell almost ran in on more than one occasion. Teams :—Aspull: Full back, Pilkington ; three-quarters, Morris, J. Seddon, and Hay- dock; half backs, Cartwright and Hulme ; forwards, Bramwell, Grundy, Bond, Monks, Smith, Dempsey, Cros- ton, Baxendale, and Hesketh. Widnes: Full back, S. Bingham; three-quarter backs, Johnson, Farrell, and Hardman; half backs, Wilkinson and Howard; for- wards, Smith, Kiddie, Hughes, Fogg, Woods, Gandy, Barber, T. Pennington, and J. Bingham. Referee, bfr. Parry. RUNCORN A TEAR V. LIVERPOOL HORNETS.—PIayed at Runcorn on Saturday, before a goodly number of spec- tators. The game was of an interesting nature, being very, fast throughout, but the home team completely outplayed their opponents, winning by 4 goals, 1 try, and 4 minor points to the Hornets two minors. The home team won the toss, and Raisbeck kicked off for the visitors, which P. Riley returned. Hampson, Jones, and Raisbeck got away with the ball to the home line, and forced Brazendale to save. Brazendale dropped out, and P. Riley and J. B. Clarke following well up carried play to the visitor's 25, when soon after, from some loose play, Lunt getting hold dropped a splendid goal. Rais- beck re-started from centre, when some grand passing was shown by Clarke, Hancock, and Gatley. The latter passed to Lunt, who sraced round his opponents and placed the ball behind the posts, Brazendale having no difficulty in placing a goal. From the kick off Brazen- dale returned, when Wadham got hold and put in a neat run tb the home quarters, WS Riley stopping his pro- gress. From a line out Riley getting hold transferred to Hollingsworth, who put in a good run to the visitors' half. From a scrimmage, the ball coming loose, Riley picked up and passed to Hancock, who threw to Lunt, the latter taking his drop at goal, the ball falling short of the crossbar, and a touchdown resulted. After the drop out Runcorn continued to press their opponents, and Andrews getting hold made a splendid run in, Bra- zendale again doing the needful. Raisbeck re-started ' from centre, Carr returned, and Stubbs. Clarke, and Gatley carried play to the visitors' lines, when Mackie picked up and cleared his lines in grand style. Wain- wright, Jones, and Raisbeck got away with a good dribble to the other end of the field, and forced Lunt to save. Half time was then called, the score standing—Runcorn, 3 goals, 2 minors, to the Hornets 2 minors. On changing ends Brazendale re-started from the centre. Walker returning. Hollingsworth put in a neat run, but Mackie and Raisbeck ran' the ball back to the home quarter. Hollingsworth again getting hold made a splendid run and came through his opponents in grand style, and was only brought down by Wainwright when close to the line. Brown here got away and saved his lines beautifully, and he throF the ha to Wain- ' wright, asho put its a §plenclist run to the other end of the field, and looked like storing when Riley brought him down. Play did net remain here long, and the home team had considerably the best of it. From now till the call of time play was kept in the visitors' quarters, An- drews and W. Riley crossing the line, the latter getting In close to touch after a grand run. Brazendale kicked a splendid goal, and after a good game the home team won as above. Teams: Runcorn—J. Brazendale, back; J. Hollingsworth, W. Riley, and E. Lunt, three-quarter backs; G. Whitby and H. G. Andrews, half backs; J. B. Clarke (captain), J. Clarke, P. Riley, W. Faulkner, J. Gatley, T. div.head: EXAM!! ' , SATURDAY, OCTOBER 22, 1887.
div.p: THE EXAM!! ' , SATURDAY, OCTOBER 22, 1887.

Eyes, Ilandalls' Craghan, Nevins, Hackett,Jones, Thorn- ley, and Walsh. Mossley—Full back, Kenworthy (cap- tain) ; -three-quarter backs, Wood, Whiteley, and Booth; half backs, Gollard and Marsden; forwards, Dawson, Sykes, W. Mellor, Batley, Hewbv, Mellor, Barker, Halli- well, and Dunkerley. WARRINGTON V. MOSSLEY. The Warrington first team journeyed to Mossley on Saturday to bring off a fixture with the club of that town. They were without the services of Jolley, who was away through indisposition, and it is needless to say that his absence was sorely felt. The home team mus- tered their full strength. The day being beautifully fine, there was no reason why a pleasant game should not be witnessed, but the sptetators were doomed to dis- appointment, for the game was exceedingly rough from the commencement to the finish. At 3-30 Frank Turner started the game agairtat a strong wind, a good return being made by Coxe. The Mossley forwards worked the leather to the Warrington quarter flag, when they ap- peared dangerous, Buxton nicely saving by kicking in touch. The visitors broke away with the ball, and a scrimmage was formed in Mossley territory. It was soon apparent that each side was determined, for a strong run by Joseph Winterbottom, and pass to Ains- worth, relieved their side to half-way. Davies spoiled Billings in a pass intended for Joseph Winterbottom, and a good kick by the latter was well returned with interest by Massey. O'Neil got in a nice punt to Massey; but from a scrimmage formed here a neat pass was made by Warren to Barnes, the latter putting in a huge kick to the home team's line. O'Neil, however again relieved his side by a short run and kick to centre-field. Passing by Warren and Fair Turner looked dan- gerous, but this effort was spoiled by the ball roiling in touch, when the last-named passed to Evans. ,Some smart tackling on the part of Littlewood foiled Jo. Winterbottom in his endeavour to get away, and play again raged in Moseley twenty-five. Marsden put in a poor kick, and for a moment it looked as if the visitors were sure to score; but Jos. Winterbottom and Ashworth, by grand runs, safely landed the ball 6ul of danger. The home team, for the first time, now pressed the Warringtonions, and from a free kick by Billinge, Hobson took the place, and from a long kick scored first minor for Moseley. Frank Turner, dropped out, add smart following up by Ashton prevented a return. The home team, by the aid of Wood and Ashworth, removed operations to neutral ground; but Massey, who played a splendid game all through, by a good kick took play again on the Mossley lines. Warren got away from the pack, butthrough rough tackling by Jos. Winterbottom the Warringtonian had, for the remaining portion of the first half, to retire. Fair. Turner went half back, and a weak pass to Barnes enabled the home team to take play to neutral ground. Davies tackled Winterbottom with the ball in his possession, and half-time was called with the score—Mossley one dead ball to Warrington nil. The wind had now subsided, and the visitors were severely handicapped through this piece of bad luck. Warren resumed his position at half back. Jamas Winterbottont re-started, no return being made, play settling in War- rington quarters. Warren made a neat run, and Percy came through a scrimmage with the ball at his toes, re- turning with a smart dribble to Mossley twenty-five. Smart passing by Speakman, Barnes, and Massey threat- ened danger., but James Winterbottom broke away, and Buxton having his kick charged down, the ball rolled in touch close to_centre flag. Povey and Fair. Turner were conspicuous by a neat dribble, but over-ran the ball when a chance of scoring seemed possible. A scrimmage being formed on the line, the visitors rushed the leather over, W. Dillon safely grounding it over the line, but the ball was ruled back, and the home team relieved the pressure to quarter flag. From the line out Ashton made away, and shortly after Massey essayed a drop at goal, the ball only falling short a few feet—hard lines, indeed, for the visitors, the home team saving by touching down. Ashton charged the drop out, and a rush by the visitors caused the Mossleyites to again adopt the saving tactics. The drop out being returned, Povey, who was playing a grand game during this half, again forced Bil- huge to touch down. Barnes returned Mayall's kick out, and from a subsequent scrimmage Mossley relieved to half way, Buxton saving this dangerous rush in grand style. A neat run by Barnes was well returned by Newby, and for the first time since the kick off the Mossleyites entered the Warrington territory. From some loose play which followed Massey got the ball away, and with a good punt to O'Neil at half-way, the latter replied to Buxton, who failed to gather the ball, and placing the Mossleyites ‘• on-side," Hobson raced upi and scored the only premier point in the match, the same player kicking a neat goal. Fair Turner re-started from centre, the ball rolling dead. Newby re-started, and Barnes made his mark, Fair Turner taking play to quar- ter flag, when the home team, " unsportsmanlike, ' re- lieved the pressure by kicking dead. The visitors played up with renewed vigour, and pressed the home team back on their lines, but could not score any legiti- mate point, and after 70 minutes' play retired defeated by one goal, one minor, to Warrington five minors. The Warrington team worked hard to a man, and, as can be seen by the score, it is apparent they had really the best of the game all through, hut not the luck. Of the backs Massey was again in his usual form, his kicking and smart running being a treat to witness. Barnes was rather roughly treated by the Severe tackling of the I home team, and, consequently, did not display his usual brilliancy. Evans was rather weak, and failed very often to relieve his side where it was most needed. Speakman was always in the thick, and rather too much for Billings. Buxton never made a mistake until he lost possession of the ball when they scored the only try of the match. To make any individual mention in the for- ward rank would be an injustice, for one and all worked hard. They completely beat their opponents, and it was, indeed, had lines for them to having so much the best of the game to have to retire defeated. 'On the Mossley side Wood, O'Neil, James Winterbottom, Walker, and Newby, were the best. The following were the teams : Warrington: Full back. J. Buxton; three-quarters, J. T. Massey, T. SAII BERNHARDT'S _IMMENSE RECEIPTS AND
PATTI'S PERIL.

Sarah Bernhardt's- receipts, for her late tour in South America, are the largest ever taken by any dramatic ar- tiste. But the reckless Sarah scarcely ever has a franc to spare! Patti has also achieved great sucecas, and a very large amount of money, in Mexico and South America, but came very near being the victim of a dynamiter, who attempted to throw an explosive bomb at her while she was singing at the Grand Opera House in San Fran- cisco' California. She was called again and again in front of the curtain when, as she was finally retiring, a man in the gallery suddenly rose, picked up a bomb from under the seat, and raising it in the air, was about to throw it, when it exploded in his hand, shattering his arm and face, and inflicting other injuries. Had the man not placed himself under the protection of a policeman, who met him as he was rushing down stairs, he would , have been torn in pieces by. the infuriated people. Patti displayed great coolness and presence of mind, and succeeded in restoring quiet by• singing "Home, Sweet Home." Poor Patti! It is a wonder she was not killed by the nervous shock, or that she did not faint, or that her hair did not turn grey through fright. Think of Patti with grey hair! Abbeautiful head of hair is the crowning glory of woman, and its loss is her greatest misfortune—a mis- fortune which may be prevented by the use of that fa- mous hair restorer and dressing, known as Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer, which will prevent bald- ness, and restore grey hair to its natural color, strength, and gloss. It can be had at any chemist's or perfumer's shop in the civilized world.

Sir H. James, M.P. for Bury, on Wednesday night ad- dressed a meeting of the Bury and Elton Liberal Unionist Association. He denied that any real concessions had been made by Mr. Gladstone, and said that if the Union- ists were now to go back to the Liberal fold it would be really an unconditional surrender. COLLISION AT SEA: ELEVEN LIVES LOST.—A Lloyd's telegram states :—The German barque Planteur has been sunk in collision with the Cork steamer Upupa. The collision occurred at 3 a.m. on Tuesday, near Ileachy Head, and the Planteur sank within a minute or two of being struck. Eleven of the crew, including the captain, his wife, and child, were drowned. The mate and one sailor were picked up by the boats of the Upupa. BOLTON Sranra.—The men's Joint Committee at Bolton have issued a manifesto in which they contend that there was nothing unreasonable in their proposal for a refer- ence to the rates of wages paid in Oldham, and add that the employers' rejection of that proposal shows that there is no desire on their part to meet the men fairly, as they have a right to expect. They declare themselves deter- mined to continue the struggle until an honourable set- tlement is arrived at, and ask for extended public sup- Pert.

LOIIDON. •THURSDAY NIGIIT. The great meeting at Nottingham, where the pulse of Liberalism has been beating so high this week, demonstrates in striking manner the sound- ness of the view of current English politics taken by an American risitor, and quoted in this column a fortnight ago. Mr. Murat Halstead, it will be re- . .

membered, being asked on his return to America how the Home Rule question was faring, answered to the effect that Home Rile was practically as- sured, but that eves more important than the pro- gress of Nome Rule was the advance of democracy. The Convention of Liberals at Nottingham has been, above all things, *democratic. The programme it has adopted, with, there is good reason to believe, the approval of the vast army of Liberals through- out Great Britain, is boldly and wisely democratic. It is a great stree beyond anything the Liberal party has hitherto formally and solemnly decided upon, and it is of immediate practical importance, since it is a moral certainty that what the Liberal' party in this country decides to do, it will before

many years, or even. months, have passed by ac- complished. It is here where, as pointed out a fortnight ago in connection with Mr. Halstead's observation, that the'crass stupidity of the Tory leaders is disclosed. Seeing no further than the end of their nose, they lent all their energies to uphold theda,ndlord in- terest in Ireland and prevent the fulfilment _of the

lic. He did not know anything about the flag. Someone had put it •in his hands, he had walked about the park and the mob had followed him ! That was all he knew about it, and the mob did not seem to know even io much.

_ That there is profound and widespread distress in London is, nevertheless, a melancholy fact not to , be obscured by mischievous vagaries of idle plat,— form spouters. The number of homeless persons who pass the night in the streets of London is sim- ply appalling. Any late passer-by along the Em- bankment will find all the benches appropriated by men (and sometimes women), who settle down there before midnight to face the long bleak night, hungry and cold, until they take their place, hun- grier and colde.r after leaving it in the morning to face another hopeless day. A curious fancy many of them have is to take their final bout of sleep in the parks. The London parks are open now at six in the morning, at which hour groups of shivering men and women gather at the gates and pass in, eager for the luxury of lying down on the wet grass. You may see them any morning, cer- tainly up to eight o'clock, sometimes later, lying all about the lawns, which they find luxuriously soft by comparison with the doorsteps or benches on which they have passed the night. The other morn- ing, in St. James s Park, I saw one figure among the scores that lay about on the grass which had interposed between itself and the wet earth, an outspread sheet of newspaper. It was not much; not equal to a fedther bed or a spring mattress, but it showed a grim hankering after comforts, perhaps more recently. possessed in his case than in that of some other or the bed-fellows with whom misfor- tune had made him acquainted. I have not read all the obituary notices of Mrs. Craik. But as far as I have seen them no note has been taken of a remarkable coincidence. Mrs. Craik died suddenly of heart disease, and so did "John Halifax, Gentleman," and so, too, did his wife. None who have rest/ the book will forget the powerful and pathetic scene of the discovery of the stricken man and of his wife, later found dead by his slue. Miss Muloch was comparatively young when "John Halifax" was written; but even then death by heart disease seems to have been a contin- gency present in her thoughts. Dr. Parker is nothing if not dramatic, and he has made the most of his opportunity during his visit to the United States. There wile one carefully re- hearsed little episode which went off with unquali- fied success. It was arranged at the Temple Church that when its beloved pastor made its first appear- ance in the pulpit lately occupied. by Mr. Beecher there should be a little sensation. The almanack was consulted to ascertain the precise difference in time between London and Brooklyn. At the ap- pointed moment, when it was known Dr. Parker would be approaching the pulpit, a message was cabled in the name of City Temple "wishing great success and God's blessing" to the preacher. Ac- cording to accounts received from New York; the little plot went off admirably. The telegraph boy 'appeared at the door of Plymouth Church just as Dr. Parker was entering the pulpit. Animated by a strict sense of duty, he would not delegate the de- livery of the message- to any deacon. It was for Dr. Parker in the pulpit at Plymouth Church, and he would deliver it himself; which he did, his ap- pearance in the pulpit side by side with the preacher " exciting," we are told, "much interest in the congregation."

.. national desire. That was all they desired to do, and it seemed natural enough that they should undertake it. But see where they have already landed themselves. Their policy of coercion and repression of national feeling has roused the British people to a pitch not reached in respect of home politics since 1868. Challenged on the one question of Home Rule for Ireland, the people, having swiftly - and irresistibly decided to concede Home Rule, do not regard their task as accomplished, and go back to their daily avocations. They have been dragged into active participation in politics, and being there mean to have a thorough look round. The Conservative leaders, who wanted nothing more than to raise again the Irish question, find that practically settled to their great discomfiture, whilst there is brought about their ears the ques- tions of Disestablishment, of Parliamentary Regis- tration, of the conveyance of voters to the poll, of one man one vote, with hints at abolition of the House of Lords. These are questions which, under more skilful treatment, might have still longer re- mained in abeyance. But the Conservative leaders have inadvertantly and maladroitly roused the latent spirit of democracy in the country, and hav- ing onoe taking its coat off the democracy can be counted upon to do a thorough day's work. Of the comparatively minor reforms added at Nottingham to the programme of the Liberal party, there are two which everyone having personal knowledge of election proceedings will recognise as of immense importance. These are the proposal to , prohibit the lending of conveyanc3s for voters, and 1 the limitation of one vote to one man. The Cor- rupt Practices Act was passed under Mr. Gladstone's Government, and in revect to the conveyance of I voters has since wrought sad havoc for the Liberal 1 cause in many constituencies. It is to Sir Henry 1 James that the Liberal party is indebted for this suicidal clause. I remember with what suspicious alacrity the proposal was assented to in Committee of the House of Commons by the Conservatives. One or two voices were raised in warning from the, Liberal side, but Sir Henry James was at the red heat of virtuous self-denial, and nothing would , satisfy him short of the absolute prohibition of 1 hiring conveyances, thus playing into the hands of 1 the party who claim to monqpolise respectability, 1 and certainly possess most of the gigs. When the ' law decrees that gratuitous conveyance of the voter to the poll under, any circumstances, is illegal, the fight will be fairer for Liberals in many a consti- tuency. The other newly-adopted war cry, "One man, one vote," strikes at another Tory strong- hold. It is a simple practical reform which we §nall Without doubt see carried in the next Perlis- 1 ment, Mr. Gladstone's reception at Nottingham and on the way there and back was sufficient by its adult), 1 tory enthusiasm to turn the head of an ordinary I man. An eye witness, Who is also familiar with scenes that took place in Midlothian during the famous campaign, and in later years, tells me that 'Edinburgh never did anything like Nottingham. There is no question that Mr. Gladstone, who little more than a year ago was talked of in Conservative circles as "played out," is now more widely popular with the masses than at any previous period of his career. At the same time things are going very badly with the old colleagues who deserted him, and some of whom have reviled him. Nobody takes any notice of Mr. Bright and his occasional flash- ings forth in petulant notelets. Lord Hartington, though he occasionally makes a speech, take par- ticular care that it shall not be delivered before his constituents at Rossendale. Mr. Courtney, making a tour through his constituency, has grown quite accustomed to have voes cf censure passed upon him at the conclusion of an able speech. Sir Henry James, paying a long-delayed visit to Bury, avoided this catastrophe by. carefully selecting his audience, who were chiefly Conservatives, and gained admis- sion to the hall by means of tickets. Like Lord Hartington, in Rossendale, and Mr. Courtney, in Cornwall, Sir Henry James has not any chance of re-election even with the Conser- vative vote. As for Mr. Chamberlain, he is even in direr straits. His seat may be safe, but his position as a public man is exceedingly embar- rassed. His policy for Ireland is repudiated from the very quarters in whose interest it was de-. liberately conceived. Neither the Orangemen of Ulster, as represented by -Dr. Kane, nor the Irish ' landlords, for whom Colonel Saunderson is spokes- man, will have anything to do with Mr. Chamber- lain's panacea for Ireland and Ulster. A still more serious matter is the prospect of his mission to the United States as British Commissioner in the forth- coming conference on the fishery question. As this morning's telegrams show, he has hopelessly aggra- vated Canada even before he actually embarks on his mission; whilst as far as the United States is concerned, he will be handicapped throughout by the bitter resentment which his recent proceedings have created among the Irishmen. The Irish vote in America is a momentous thing, and American statesmen, coming in contact with Mr. Chamberlain will have it threateningly before them in any corn-. munication with him. This is very bad for Mr. Chamberlain; hat, worse still, it is very unfortunate 1 for the country which he will represent. The encounters between the unemployed and the police of London loom much larger in newspaper reports than in actual fact. There are, undoubtedly, immense crowds ,gathered, whether in Trafalgar- square, Hyde Park, or on the embankment. But a large proportion of those present are drawn by cu- riosity. Being unemployed, as too many people in London are just now, they think it will help to pass the time if they flock to see what is going on in Tra- falgar-square. But there is nothing in the way of organised resistance to law and order. With a sub- stratum of saddening 'fact there is something irre- sistibly comical in the episodes of the daily demon- stration. The wildest device of the pantomime season could not produce anything more surpris- ingly and riotously funny than the experience of the man OlcUand at Monday's meeting. He was a Principal person., in the morning's demonstration. lie was one of tlie six deputed to take counsel with the Lord Mayor, He loftily harangued the sitting magistrate at the Mansion House, and going back to report on his mission to the waiting mob in Tra- falgar-square, was himself suddenly set up, buffeted, and literally kicked out of the square. Marat and Robespierre in the French revolutionary times hada longer spell of power than this. Another significant and ludicrous incident came ont in the police court proceedings where a boy of sixteen was brought up, charged with uplifting the flag of ,the Red Repub..

div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. A_special meeting of the Widnes Local Board was

'held. on Tuesday, under the presidency of Mr. F. H. Gossage. Present—Messrs. J. Midwood, J. Taylor, B. Cook, H. Gaskell, 3unr.,lE. Carey, J. Houghton, W. W. Gossage, D. Wright, S. Sadler, and J. T. Allen (clerk). THE ANNUAL LICENSING SESSION: PROPOSED REMOVAL. —The Clerk read the following letter from Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner :—" As the magistrates have made Widnes a petty sessional division, would it not be as well to requisition them to have the general annual and quarterly licensing sassions held in Widnes for the district, instead of at Prescot, as heretofore. I shall be glad if you will kindly bring this matter before your Board."—The Chairman: Why doesn't Mr. Hus- band advocate this matter personally ?—Mr. Wright: He is not a member.—The Chairman: I suppose it is to save people the trouble of going to Prescot by allowing them to get licenses from the magistrates. here.—Mr. Gaskell did not know whether the Board ought to take action at the instigation of one individual without an intimation from the ratepayers that the change was wanted. Widnes was not a division' the town was still a portion of Prescot division, and a change would mean that the whole of the licensing sessions would have to be 'held in Widnes.—The Clerk said Mr. Husband's idea was that that portion of Prescot division which was now represented by the police division of Widnes should have a separate licensing session. He had been speaking to one or two gentlemen, and he had been told that this could be done if the townspeople desired it.—The Chairman said Mr. Allen had better in- quire from Mr. Husband what were the grounds for making this request. A licensing session at Widnes would be a great convenience.—lt was decided that the discussion should be adjourned to the monthly meeting, Mr. Allen, in the meantime, to obtain what information he could. THE PROPOSED FREE LECTURES.—The Clerk said the Free Library Committee proposed to organise a series of free lectures during the winter at a cost of £l5, and as such a scheme was not provided for in the Libraries Act of 1855, he was instructed to ask the sanction of the Local Government Board under the Act passed last year so that there might be no risk of surcharge. The Local Government Board had written as follows :—"The Board have considered this matter, and they think that the application should be made by the Local Board, and not by the Public Library Committee. The committee did not appear to be a local authority within the mean- ing of the Act 50, 51 Vic., c. 72. Your letter of the 30th September did not contain sufficient information to justify the Board in promising to sanction the proposed expenditure. But looking to the full explanation you have since forwarded, there seems some ground for the contention that the Local Board could carry out their scheme under the Free Librar- ies Act. This point, however, is open to doubt, and to remove any difficulty the Board are prepared to receive an application from the Local Board, and to sanction the expenditure of a sum not exceeding £l5 for the purpose in question."— The Chairman observed that the course of lectures would increase the usefulness of the Board, and on the motion of Mr. Carey, seconded by Mr. Midwood, it was resolved that the Clerk should make the necessary application.

Advanced stage A. D. Whitby; 2nd, Thomas Walker. RE-OPENING OF RUNCORN PARIS 4 CIIURCII MEMORIAL TO CANON BARCLAY. After being closed several weeks for renovation and repairs, Runcorn Parish Church was re-opened , on Thursday evening. The stone work and wood work of the interior of the sacred edifice has been thoroughly cleaned, whilst the walls have been painted in a pretty pale blue colour A great im- provement has been effected in making the floor ot , the chancel of one uniform level, and the choir ' stalls having been widened will add to the comfort of the choristers. An addition has been made to the furniture of the church in the shape of a prayer desk, which is placed on the opposite side of the chancel to the pulpit. Thecorona which formerly ' gave light to the chancel has been taken'clown, and replaced by several standards. Notwithstanding ; numerous difficulties, the work has been expediti- ously- and admirably carried out by Messrs. T. Kirkham and Co., and the beauty of the ancient fabric is considerably heightened by the thorough overhauling it has had. The cost of the entire work is about .2140, and we believe that the Vicar, the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, in- tends to become personally responsible for the amount. Whilst Messrs. Kirkham were carrying out their contract, the firm of Messrs. Williams and Clay, sculptors, kc., of Warrington, have erected the memo- rial tablet to the late Vicar. It will be remembered that shortly after the death of Canon Barclay a meeting of parishioners determined to perpetuate his memory by a monument, and a committee, having the Rev. A. Mait- land Wood as chairman, the late Mr. Chorlton, treasu- rer, and Messrs. W. Sutton and G. Moss as secretaries, was appointed to collect subscriptions. Upwards of £lOO was obtained. Competition drawings of a tablet were then invited, and that sent in by Messrs. Williams and Clay was adjudged the best and accepted. The de- sign is that of Mr. T. Beesley, architect, Bold-street, Warrington. The tablet, which has been placed on the right of the chancel, is executed in ala- baster and statuary marble, elaborately carved and moulded, and is a beautiful work of art. The style adopted is gothic. It consists of three panels CT compartments, a large central gable with traceried canopies each side, beneath which are placed two statu- ettes, carved in white statuary marble, representing " eloquence " and "industry." In the niche forming the centre there is a deeply moulded arch, supported on green marble columns with foliated capitals. In this a medallion portrait of the late canon is fixed, carved in statuary marble. The fidelity of the likeness is striking, and more than realises the anticipations of the commit- tee. The whole is surmounted with a moulded coping, enriched with crock, and finished with an inlaid cross.! The tablet is fixed next the chancel arch, posite the pulpit, about seven feet from the floor, and measures

• bout eight feet six inches high by four feet wide. The 1 nscription, which is neatly cut in bold letteis and en- amelled in black, is as follows :—" john Barclay, ILA., of Christ Church, Oxford, vicar of Runcorn for nearly 41 years, rural dean of Frodsham, proctorin Convocation, and hon. canon of Chester Cathedral. Born Dec. 25,1816, died August 25th, 1886. A man of wisdom, learning, elo- quence, power, industry, and zeal, who had earned in his Master's service the love of his people as teacher, guide, and father." On the panel at the bottom of the tablet is cut the words, "This monument is erected by the parishioners in gratitude to God for him and his work." There was a crowded congregation at the re- opening service on Thursday evening, when the monu- ment was first exposed to the public gaze. The prayers were read by the Vicar, and the lessons by the Rev. W. Bryant and the Rev. Tindall, curates. The Rev. E. 0. Rawson, M.A., vicar of Ince, preached an appropriate sermon. During the service the choir sang the anthem "This is the day," the solo being capitally rendered by Mr. James Littler.

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Town Hall, Widnes, on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. T. S. Timmis presided, and there were present the Revs. Dean Finegan, Father Clarke, and George I Bond; Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Bradshaw, Imison, Dea- con, Heyes, Wareing, and Danby (clerk.)

DISTRICT -EDUCATION COMMITTEE. The District Education Committee reported that dur- ing September (five weeks) there were 136 applications for school fees, and they were recommended to be paid in 124 cases. There were 262 persons summoned before the Committee for contravention of the Education Act, and 71 were prosecuted before the magistrates, seventy were convicted, and one child was sent to an industrial , school.
A YEAR'S WORE.

Mr. Deacon presented a report of the work of the District Education Committee for the year ended August 31st, 1887. The following is a comparison of the past fiVe years :- 1883. 1884. 1885. 1886. 1887. Average number on rolls. 5223 5464.5 5737'1 59575 6223-6 Average attendance Percentage Mr. Deacon referred to the percentage of attendants. and expressed the opinion that compulsion would never raise the figure beyond the present point. The com- mittee had thoroughly attended to this work, and had without fear or favour prosecuted in cases where they thought prosecution justified. Since 1884 they had made no perceptible advance in the percentage of attendance, and it seemed to him some fillip of a different sort was needed to get the figures beyond the magical 80 per cent or thereabout. How this was to be given he was not pre- pared to say, but he must admit that he did not expect much from compulsion in the future. The 80 per cent. really meant that in Widnes each day there were 1,200 children absent from school who ought to be in atten- dance. If anybody could suggest a better method of , Carrying out the Education Act, and of increasing this I perEentage the committed would behatndato recerve such a suggestion.—ln reply to the cr it, Mr. Deacon said in many large towns the average was about 80 per cent.—Father Clarke said he knew that the epidemic of , measles had kept hundreds of children away from school that otherwise would have been therd.—Father, Finegan concurred, and said they were all sorry that the efforts of the committee had not been more successful.— The Chairman said no doubt the explanation given by Father Clarke of the decrease of the percentage was Ithe correct one, and could not be accounted for by any failure on the part of the committee. They all knew how painstaking the committee had been in fulfilling its duties. He moved the adoption of the report with thanks to the committee.—Father Finegan seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.

div.head: GENEROSITY OF MR. BOLTON.
div.p: GENEROSITY OF MR. BOLTON.

The Chairman said he had received a letter from Mr. G. H. Bolton, of the Widnes Alkali Company. It would be in the recollection of the Board that Mr. Bolton last year generously gave the school children a trip to Liver- pool Exhibition, and he proposed to again take a thou- sand scholars to the Manchester Exhibition.—The Clerk then read the letter making the offer. Mr. Bolton asked the Board to give the children a general holiday, so that those who were not selected to visit the Exhibition would not feel the disappointment so keenly.—Dean Finegan moved, and Father Clarke seconded, a motion that a letter of thanks be forwarded to Mr. Bolton, and that the children be given a holiday as requested.—The Chairman remarked that the offer was an extremely generous one, and the resolution was carried imam- mously.

THE ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER AT STOCKTON HEATH. On Tuesday, at the Sessions House, at Warring- ton, before Mr. J. C. Parr, John Hart, described as a horse dealer, of Runcorn, was brought up bn remand on a charge of having caused the death of Joseph William Newton, his brother-in-law, at Stockton Heath, on the 19th of July last. Mr. A. Browne ap- peared for the defence.—William Arthur Cook, bcoat- man, Stockton Heath, said that he remembered the night of the 19th of July last. At about eleven o'clock he heard a disturbance in the street, and saw John Hart knocking at the door of Newton's house. Newton came out and said, " John' I want no bother here. Tom's not had here." The two ad a few words, and then went in- side the house. When they were outside there was no fall and witness could not perceive that Newton was injured in any way. A few minutes afterwards witness , heard screams of murder proceed from the house, and , aftet an interval of about five minutes Newton came out ' and spoke to witness. Newton's head was then bleed- ing, and there was a bandage round it. Mrs. Newton had come to the door and called out to prisoner, who was , about fifteen yards from the house, "Jack, thall have Ito catch it for this, if you are my brother, for he is my ipoor husband." In answer to Mr. Browne, witness said ' that there were no lights in the shops. Prisoner's mother I lived at the house next but one to Newton's house. i Witness did not know that prisoner and his brother Tom I had been quarrelling. The pavement near Newton's ihouse was made of cobbles, and there was a kerbstone. IWitness did not see Newton push John Hart, nor did he I see Newton on the ground.—Annie Wilks, wife of Thos. , Wilks, Stockton Heath, said that on the night in ques- tion John Hart, who was singing, passed her house. She I then heard someone kicking at a door, and went to the , door of her own house. In consequence of a noise that I she heard in Newton's house she went to the kitchen ' window of that house. There was alight, either from a !candle or the fire. There were id the kitchen William Newton, John Hart, Tom Hart, and Mrs. Newton. They were quarreling. Witness saw John Hart lift his hand , to strike someone, and Newton went to the door leading I into the front kitchen. John Hart, when he lifted his , hand had something in it, about eight or niie inches , long. Witness heard a woman's voice say, "Oh, good God, what's tha done." She then went back to her own , house, and prisoner tried to get in. He said "See, ! missus, they ve stabbed me." Cross-examined by Mr. I Browne, witness said that she afterwards heard prisoner I say that he had been robbed of £l3 10s. She did not I attend the inquest because she was afraid to do so.—Dr. lArgo, Stretton, said that on the sth of August he re- ceived an order from the 1 relieving. officer to attend the deceased. He found him suffering from a cut on his • head, which did not appear to be a recent wound. Wit- ness continued to attend deceased until the time of his I death, which occurred on the 30th of September. The • deceased's skull was fractured, and his death was caused by compression of the brain, followed by general paralysis. The wound could have been caused by a fall. Witness had several conversations with the deceased, who did not seem to bear any ill-will towards the prisoner.—El- len Percival, Stockton Heath, and others, also gave evid- ence, ; ence and the magistrate had a short consultation with the clerk, after which Mr. Parr said he did not , think there was sufficient evidence to convict.—Prisone: i was therefore discharged.—We understand that a copy ' of a statement voluntarily made by the deceased on the ' 29th of August, signed by himself, and by Mr. James ' Whitley, Stockton Heath, and Alice Newton, as wit 2 I nesses, was submitted to his Worship. The statement was as follows :—" I, William Newton, of Stockton ;Heath, do here declare solemnly before God and these l' witnesses here present that on the 18th (?) day of July last, i about half-past ten in the evening, John Hart came on .I my doorstep. I had my shoes off, and we were just go- , ' ing to bed, and I was under the impression that there ' would be some unpleasantness between him and his 1 brother o John Hart, d eor Thomas, awhoawoas pushed hi then in my house. away . Ifropmut my h ' door, and in doing so I slipped down. I was not pushed down by anyone. I got up and came into the house and locked the door. I believe that in falling down I hurt my head on some sharp-edged stones which Were lying close to my door. I do not lay any blame to any per- son or persons for the wound At the back of my head."

It is really cf vital importance that every facility should be afforded to our youth to cultivate their powers to the utmost. Our larger towns, which see more clearly the signs of the times, have long since granted their inhabitants the boon which we now claim as our right. In addition to this they have established evening classes for the study of all kinds of subjects, classes to which our owmyouths are forced to go at great expense through the shortsightedness and supineness of our local rulers. The question of education is Becoming a most serious problem to middle-cla.ss youths, and it behoves all who have the,welfare of the town and country at heart to see that they have no obstacles placed in their paths. Fields that the middle-class once regarded as peculiarly is own are now invaded, first by the Ger- man who s better educated, and next by the sons of the working-class who are quite as well educated now-a- days, and between these two the middle-class youths have, and will have, a keen struggle for supremacy. It is, therefore, necessary to their very existence that our youths should be enabled to take full . advantage of all local institutions of an educational character, and I would urge our Town Councillors to think of this phase of the subject when they vote on Tuesday next. We in Warrington, cannot afford to be behind our , neighbours in any respect, and the sooner we are put on the same footing respecting the Free Library the better. Why there should be a charge at our library I entirely fail to see, and lain confident if the Library Comnaittee. would only bring themselves to try even the experiment ,lof a Free Library for a few years they would be abun- dantly satisfied with its success frolt every point of view. I appeal, therefore, to our Town Councillors to show next Tuesday that- they have the welfare of the ratepayers at heart by voting in favour of a policy that shall put all who use the library upon a perfect I October 18th, 1887. GLADSTONE.—Mr. Gladstone, says a:Central News correspondent at Sudbury, spent a quiet day on Friday. His voice was very weak after the exertions of the last few days, but otherwise he was in excellent health and spirits. Mr, Gladstone Stays at Sudbury until Monday, when he will go to Ripon. Lord Randolph Churchill, addressing delegates from the Seaharn Hs,rboirr Primrose League and Conservative Association, at Chester-le-Street, near Newcastle, on Friday 'aftattoon, spoke in eulogistic terms of Lord Londonderry's Government of Ireland, holding that it compared most favourably with that of Lord Aber- deen.

A WELL-To-Do PerPER.—At a meeting of the New- castle-on-Tyne Guardians on Friday afternoon it was re- ported that the sum of £4OO in bank notes had been dis- covered sewn up in the clothes of a pauper lunatic, who had been removed from the Workhouse to the asylum. The money was lodged in the bank in the name of the Guardians.

A Heumrr's WILL.—A shocking discovery was re cently made at Oswaldtwistle. An old man, named Thomas Butterworth, aged 82, who had lived alone for 30 years, had not been seen for three weeks. His house was broken into, and his dead body was found horribly decomposed. A will made by deceased has been found showing personal estate of the value of £986. PROVINCIAL GRAND LODGE OF CHESEIRE.—OR Friday Lord Egerton of Tatton, Right Worshipful Provincial Grand blaster, opened the Provincial Grand. Lodge at Crewe. MS lordship was accompanied by his Honour Judge Horatio Lloyd, D.P.G.M., the Hon. Alan de Tat- ton Egerton, M.P., and a large number of members of the craft from Manchester, Chester; Liverpool, and dis- trict.

DECAPITATED ON THE RAILWAY.—A shocking fatality occurred on the railway at Clitheroe on Friday morning. A man named Thomas Heaps was found decapitated. ' Ms head was cut clear off, and found 20 yards from the body. One arm was also cut off. The deceased appeared about 60 years of age. Evidence points to the case being one of suicide, but nothing is known as to how he got on the line. PAINFUL DISCOVERY AT A COLLIERY.—EarIy in 1881 disastrous explosion occurred at the Whitefield Colliery, North Staffordshire, worked by the Chatterly Iron and Coal Company, and 21 men and boys were entombed. On Friday afternoon the miners in sinking a new shaft, 450 yards deep, came across a place where their dead com- rades lie, and brought four bodies to the surface, whilst fragments of human remains are constantly being dis- covered.

THE FREE LIBRARY. Sir,—As the last meeting of the municipal year is to be held on Tuesday next, I hope the members will make it a memorable one in the records of local history by com- pletely freeing the library from its present monetary barriers, and thus enabling it to enter upon a full career of usefulness in this tever-to-be-forgotten Jubilee year. So far, Warrington has done nothing worthy of itself in the way of commemorating this great historic year.
